questions.prompt:
The recommended daily intake of vitamin C for an adult man is 90 mg. Cooked broccoli contains 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 g.

Calculate the mass of cooked broccoli a man would need to eat to get his recommended daily intake. (2)
hints: How many lots of 30 mg make 90 mg?

questions.prompt:
A woman needs 75 mg of vitamin C a day. Raw red pepper contains 125 mg per 100 g, and cooking reduces this by 40 %.

Calculate the mass of cooked red pepper she would need to eat. (2)
hints: First find the vitamin C in 100 g of cooked pepper.
questions.solution:
Cooked pepper contains 125 × 0.6 = 75 mg per 100 g [M1]
So 100 g is needed [A1]

questions.prompt:
Boiled cabbage contains 18 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. Raw cabbage contains 36 mg per 100 g.

Calculate the percentage decrease in vitamin C when cabbage is boiled. (2)
hints: The original value is the raw cabbage.

questions.prompt:
Chitin is a polysaccharide in fungal cell walls. Its monomers are like β-glucose but have an extra side group containing nitrogen (eight carbon atoms in total). Neighbouring monomers are inverted and joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds.

Compare and contrast the structure of chitin with the structure of cellulose. (3)
hints: Give at least one similarity and one difference.
Look at the bonds, the orientation of monomers and the atoms present.
questions.solution:
Similarity: both joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds [B1]
Similarity: in both, alternate monomers are inverted / both form straight chains [B1]
Difference: chitin monomers have 8 carbons, cellulose (β-glucose) has 6 [B1]
Difference: chitin contains nitrogen, cellulose does not [B1]
Any 3, including at least one similarity and one difference — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the structures of amylose and amylopectin. (3)
hints: Think about branching and bond types.
questions.solution:
Similarity: both are polymers of α-glucose [B1]
Similarity: both contain 1,4 glycosidic bonds [B1]
Difference: amylose is unbranched and coils into a helix; amylopectin is branched [B1]
Difference: amylopectin also has 1,6 glycosidic bonds at the branches [B1]
Any 3, including at least one similarity and one difference — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of glycogen makes it a suitable energy store in animals. (3)
hints: Animals need glucose quickly for respiration.
questions.solution:
Highly branched, so many ends for enzymes to hydrolyse glucose from quickly [B1]
Compact / coiled, so a lot stored in a small space [B1]
Insoluble, so does not affect water potential / osmosis [B1]
Large, so cannot diffuse out of cells [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Thrombin is formed from prothrombin when a blood vessel is damaged.

Describe the role of thrombin in blood clotting. (3)
hints: Thrombin is an enzyme. What is its substrate?
What does fibrin form, and what does it trap?
questions.solution:
Thrombin is an enzyme [B1]
It converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin [B1]
Fibrin forms a mesh of fibres [B1]
That traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of platelets in the formation of a blood clot. (3)
hints: What do platelets do when they meet collagen?
questions.solution:
Platelets stick to exposed collagen at the damaged vessel wall / form a platelet plug [B1]
They release thromboplastin (and serotonin) [B1]
Thromboplastin (with calcium ions) catalyses the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin [B1]
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which forms the clot mesh [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how atherosclerosis can lead to a blood clot forming inside a coronary artery. (3)
hints: Start with damage to the endothelium.
What makes the clotting cascade start inside an artery?
questions.solution:
Endothelium is damaged (e.g. by high blood pressure / toxins) [B1]
Inflammatory response: white blood cells and cholesterol build up to form an atheroma / plaque [B1]
Plaque may rupture, exposing collagen [B1]
Platelets stick and the clotting cascade starts, forming a thrombus [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Catalase released 90 mm³ of oxygen in 1 minute at 20 °C and 225 mm³ at 30 °C.

Calculate the temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) for this reaction between 20 °C and 30 °C. (1)
hints: Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10) ÷ rate at T.
Divide the 30 °C value by the 20 °C value.

questions.prompt:
The rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction was 12 units at 15 °C. Its Q₁₀ is 2.0.

Predict the rate at 25 °C. (1)
hints: Q₁₀ tells you how many times faster per 10 °C rise.

questions.prompt:
The heart rate of a water flea was 150 beats per minute at 10 °C and 330 beats per minute at 20 °C.

Calculate the Q₁₀. (1)
hints: Rate at the higher temperature ÷ rate at the lower.

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing the temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C increases the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. (3)
hints: Think about kinetic energy and collisions.
What forms when substrate enters the active site?
questions.solution:
Molecules gain more kinetic energy / move faster [B1]
More frequent collisions between enzyme and substrate [B1]
More enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time [B1]
More molecules have the activation energy (enzyme not yet denatured) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction falls at temperatures above the optimum. (3)
hints: What happens to bonds in the enzyme?
Link the change of shape to the substrate.
questions.solution:
Vibrations break hydrogen / ionic bonds in the enzyme [B1]
The tertiary structure / shape of the active site changes (denaturation) [B1]
The substrate no longer fits the active site / is not complementary [B1]
So fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Between 40 °C and 50 °C, the volume of oxygen released by catalase in 1 minute fell from 520 mm³ to 300 mm³.

Calculate the Q₁₀ and explain what the value shows. (3)
hints: What does a value below 1 mean?
questions.solution:
Q₁₀ = 300 ÷ 520 = 0.58 [B1]
Value below 1 shows the rate decreases as temperature rises [B1]
Because the enzyme is being denatured / active site changes shape [B1]
So fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: State one difference between the hexose sugar in cellulose and the hexose sugar in amylopectin. (1)
hints: Look at the position of the OH on carbon 1.
questions.solution: Cellulose is made of β-glucose; amylopectin is made of α-glucose (OH on carbon 1 is above / below the ring) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the two monosaccharides that make up sucrose. (1)
hints: The other is a fruit sugar.
questions.solution: Glucose and fructose [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of bond that forms at a branch point in amylopectin. (1)
questions.solution: 1,6 glycosidic bond [B1]

questions.prompt:
The mean mass of adult men in one country is 84 kg and the mean height is 1.78 m.

Calculate the mean BMI and state the weight category (healthy 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obese 30+). (2)
A woman is 1.60 m tall. Calculate the maximum mass she can have to stay in the healthy BMI range (up to 24.9). (2)
Give two reasons why waist-to-hip ratio can be a better indicator of cardiovascular risk than BMI. (2)
hints: BMI doesn't distinguish muscle from fat.
questions.solution:
BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat (muscular people may appear overweight) [B1]
Waist-to-hip ratio shows abdominal / visceral fat, which is more strongly linked to CVD [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the atrioventricular valves work during one cardiac cycle. (2)
hints: Valves open and close because of pressure differences.
questions.solution:
AV valves open when pressure in the atria is higher than in the ventricles, so blood flows into the ventricles [B1]
They close when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure (ventricular systole), preventing backflow [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the semilunar valves work during one cardiac cycle. (2)
hints: They are at the base of the arteries.
When does ventricular pressure exceed arterial pressure?
questions.solution:
Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure is greater than pressure in the aorta / pulmonary artery [B1]
They close when ventricles relax and arterial pressure is higher, preventing backflow into the ventricles [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. (2)
hints: Where does each ventricle pump blood?
questions.solution:
Left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body / systemic circulation; right only to the lungs [B1]
So it must contract more forcefully to generate higher pressure [B1]

questions.prompt:
The pulmonary vein carries blood at low pressure from the lungs to the heart. It has no valves.

Explain how its structure differs from that of the pulmonary artery and how this relates to its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Vein has a thinner wall with less muscle and elastic tissue, as blood is at low pressure [B1]
Vein has a wider lumen to reduce resistance to blood flow [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Thick wall with smooth muscle and elastic fibres to withstand high pressure [B1]
Elastic tissue stretches and recoils, smoothing blood flow / maintaining pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a capillary is related to its function. (2)
questions.solution:
Wall one cell thick (endothelium), giving a short diffusion distance [B1]
Narrow lumen / many branches give a large surface area and slow flow for exchange [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which substance do platelets release at the site of a damaged blood vessel?

Choose one answer.

A  Fibrin
B  Prothrombin
C  Thrombin
D  Thromboplastin (1)
hints: It is an enzyme released from platelets.
questions.solution: D — thromboplastin. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which enzyme converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin?

Choose one answer.

A  Fibrinogen
B  Prothrombin
C  Thrombin
D  Thromboplastin (1)
hints: Ends in -in but is an enzyme.
questions.solution: C — thrombin. [B1]

questions.prompt: Which ion is needed for prothrombin to be converted to thrombin? (1)
hints: It is also needed for muscle contraction.
questions.solution: Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Female mice in group P had raised HDL and produced a mean of 0.5 offspring per month. Group Q had the same genetic modification plus a drug that lowered HDL to normal, and produced 3.8 per month. Group R (drug only, normal HDL) produced 4.0 per month.

Comment on the effect of HDL on fertility. (4)
hints: Does the drug itself affect fertility?
questions.solution:
High HDL is associated with lower fertility (P much lower than Q and R) [B1]
Lowering HDL with the drug restored fertility to near normal (Q ≈ R) [B1]
Drug alone had little effect, so the change in Q is due to lower HDL, not the drug [B1]
Need statistical test / error bars; mice may not represent humans; only one genetic modification [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and role of HDLs and LDLs. (4)
hints: Which carries cholesterol to the liver?
questions.solution:
HDLs contain more protein than lipid; LDLs contain more lipid than protein [B1]
HDLs are denser than LDLs [B1]
HDLs carry cholesterol from tissues to the liver for removal [B1]
LDLs carry cholesterol from the liver to tissues; high LDL linked to atheroma [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a diet high in saturated fat increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. (4)
questions.solution:
Saturated fat raises blood LDL levels [B1]
LDL cholesterol is deposited in damaged artery walls [B1]
Atheroma / plaque forms, narrowing the lumen [B1]
Raised blood pressure / risk of clot, leading to heart attack or stroke [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how lactose is formed from two monosaccharides. (2)
questions.solution:
Glucose and galactose join [B1]
In a condensation reaction forming a (1,4) glycosidic bond, releasing water [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how maltose is formed. (2)
questions.solution:
Two α-glucose molecules [B1]
Joined by a condensation reaction forming a 1,4 glycosidic bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people who lack the enzyme lactase have symptoms when they drink milk. (2)
hints: What happens to it in the large intestine?
questions.solution:
Lactose is not hydrolysed into glucose and galactose, so is not absorbed [B1]
Bacteria in the large intestine ferment it, producing gas / diarrhoea / bloating [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a peptide bond is formed. (2)
hints: Which groups on the two amino acids react?
What is the name of the reaction?
questions.solution:
Condensation reaction (releasing water) [B1]
Between the amine group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a dipeptide is broken down into amino acids. (2)
hints: It is the reverse of how it was formed.
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis reaction / water is added [B1]
The peptide bond is broken (catalysed by a protease / peptidase) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a change in one amino acid can change the shape of a protein. (2)
hints: Which bonds hold the tertiary structure?
questions.solution:
The R group is different, so different bonds form (hydrogen, ionic, disulfide bridges) [B1]
So the folding / tertiary structure changes [B1]

questions.prompt:
A mutation in the gene for clotting factor V produces a factor V protein that stays active for longer than normal. Factor V helps convert prothrombin to thrombin.

Explain why people with this mutation have an increased risk of blood clots. (3)
hints: How does a gene mutation change the protein?
Follow the chain through to thrombin and fibrin.
questions.solution:
The mutation changes the base sequence / so a different amino acid sequence (primary structure) [B1]
So the protein's shape changes and it is not broken down / inactivated as quickly [B1]
More prothrombin is converted to thrombin [B1]
So more fibrin forms / clots form more easily [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
People with haemophilia have a mutation in the gene for a clotting factor.

Explain why this mutation causes bleeding that is hard to stop. (3)
hints: What happens to the shape of the protein?
If one step of the cascade fails, what can't be made?
questions.solution:
The mutation alters the base sequence, so the amino acid sequence of the clotting factor changes [B1]
The protein folds differently / is non-functional [B1]
So less thrombin / fibrin is produced [B1]
So clots form slowly or not at all [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a substitution mutation sometimes has no effect on the protein produced. (3)
hints: Where in the protein is the change?
questions.solution:
The genetic code is degenerate — several triplets code for the same amino acid [B1]
So the new triplet may code for the same amino acid (silent mutation) [B1]
Or the new amino acid may have similar properties / be outside the active site, so the shape is unaffected [B1]
Or the mutation is in a non-coding region / intron [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Batten disease is an inherited recessive disorder.

Explain what is meant by an inherited recessive disorder. (2)
hints: It is caused by a faulty allele passed from parents.
When is a recessive allele expressed?
questions.solution:
Caused by a (faulty) allele passed on from parents [B1]
Only expressed when two copies are present / homozygous recessive (no dominant normal allele) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the term carrier in relation to cystic fibrosis. (2)
questions.solution:
A person who is heterozygous / has one recessive CF allele and one normal allele [B1]
Does not have symptoms but can pass the allele on to children [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis can have a child who does. (2)
hints: What genotype must the child have?
questions.solution:
Both parents are carriers / heterozygous [B1]
The child inherits a recessive allele from each parent, so is homozygous recessive [B1]

questions.prompt:
Two unaffected parents have a child with Batten disease.

Draw a genetic diagram to show the probability that their next child will have Batten disease. Use B for the normal allele and b for the faulty allele. (2)
hints: Draw a Punnett square of the gametes.
questions.solution:
Parents Bb × Bb; gametes B, b and B, b; offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb [M1]
Probability = 1 in 4 / 0.25 / 25 % [A1]

questions.prompt:
A man with cystic fibrosis (ff) has children with a woman who is a carrier (Ff).

Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that their child will be a carrier. (2)
hints: The man can only make f gametes.
questions.solution:
Gametes f and F, f; offspring Ff, ff (in equal numbers) [M1]
Probability of a carrier = 1 in 2 / 0.5 / 50 % [A1]

questions.prompt:
Two carriers of cystic fibrosis have a child who does not have the disease.

Calculate the probability that this child is a carrier. Show your working. (2)
hints: Only consider children without the disease.
Of FF, Ff, Ff, how many are carriers?
questions.solution:
Offspring of Ff × Ff: FF, Ff, Ff, ff; unaffected = FF, Ff, Ff [M1]
Probability of carrier = 2/3 (0.67) [A1]

questions.prompt:
Several types of genetic screening are available: carrier testing of adults, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS), non-invasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD) and preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) during IVF.

Assess the advantages and disadvantages of these types of screening for a couple at risk of having a child with a recessive genetic disorder. (6)
hints: Compare risk of miscarriage, timing and accuracy.
questions.solution:
Carrier testing tells the couple their risk before conceiving, with no risk to a fetus [B1]
Amniocentesis (15–20 weeks) has about a 1 % miscarriage risk and gives results late, making termination decisions harder [B1]
CVS can be done earlier (10–13 weeks) but has a slightly higher miscarriage risk [B1]
NIPD uses fetal DNA in the mother's blood — no miscarriage risk, but less widely available / may need confirming [B1]
PGD tests embryos before implantation, avoiding termination, but IVF is expensive, has low success rates and raises ethical issues about discarding embryos [B1]
Judgement, e.g. adult carrier testing followed by NIPD or PGD is preferable because the risks are lowest [B1]
Level-marked: a full answer covers advantages and disadvantages of several methods with a supported judgement (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Discuss the ethical issues raised by the use of prenatal genetic testing. (6)
hints: Consider the fetus, the parents and society.
questions.solution:
Testing lets parents prepare or make informed decisions [B1]
May lead to termination of pregnancy — some believe the fetus has a right to life [B1]
Invasive tests (amniocentesis / CVS) risk miscarriage of a healthy fetus [B1]
False positives / negatives may lead to wrong decisions [B1]
Concern about 'designer babies' / discrimination against people with disabilities [B1]
Who decides which conditions are tested for / cost to health services [B1]
Level-marked: a balanced discussion with several points on both sides (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Cystic fibrosis could be treated by gene therapy, using liposomes or viruses to deliver normal CFTR alleles to cells lining the airways.

Evaluate gene therapy as a treatment for cystic fibrosis. (6)
hints: Somatic gene therapy only affects the cells treated.
Think about delivery problems as well as benefits.
questions.solution:
Normal allele is expressed, so functional CFTR protein is made and mucus becomes less sticky [B1]
Somatic therapy — only affects body cells, not passed to children [B1]
Airway cells are constantly replaced, so treatment must be repeated [B1]
Hard to get the allele into enough cells / mucus blocks delivery [B1]
Viral vectors may trigger an immune response; liposomes are less efficient [B1]
Judgement: promising but not yet a reliable cure; reduces symptoms only temporarily [B1]
Level-marked: a balanced evaluation with a supported judgement (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Which component of the cell surface membrane allows ions such as Na⁺ to cross it?

Choose one answer.

A  Cholesterol
B  Glycolipid
C  Channel protein
D  Phospholipid tail (1)
hints: Ions are charged, so cannot pass through the hydrophobic core.
Which component forms a water-filled pore?
questions.solution: C — channel protein. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a diagram the width of a phospholipid bilayer is 3.0 cm. The actual width is 7.5 nm.

Calculate the magnification of the diagram. (1)
hints: Convert 3.0 cm to nm (1 cm = 10⁷ nm).

questions.prompt: Name one component of the cell surface membrane that has both a hydrophilic and a hydrophobic region. (1)
hints: Think about molecules that sit across or within the bilayer.
Phosphate heads and fatty acid tails behave differently in water.
questions.solution: Phospholipid (or glycolipid / cholesterol / intrinsic protein) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids arrange themselves as a bilayer in the cell surface membrane. (3)
hints: Which parts of a phospholipid are attracted to water?
There is water inside and outside the cell.
questions.solution:
Phosphate head is hydrophilic / polar [B1]
Fatty acid tails are hydrophobic / non-polar [B1]
Water is present on both sides of the membrane (cytoplasm and tissue fluid) [B1]
So heads face outwards towards water and tails point inwards, away from water [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the cell surface membrane is described as a fluid mosaic. (3)
hints: What can the phospholipids and proteins do?
questions.solution:
Fluid: phospholipids (and proteins) can move about / diffuse within the bilayer [B1]
Mosaic: proteins are scattered through the bilayer [B1]
Like tiles in a mosaic / in a pattern that keeps changing [B1]
Cholesterol / temperature / unsaturated fatty acids affect the fluidity [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose cannot simply diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer, and how it does cross the membrane. (3)
questions.solution:
Glucose is polar / water-soluble, so is repelled by the hydrophobic core of the bilayer [B1]
It is too large to pass between phospholipids [B1]
It crosses by facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins [B1]
Or by active transport / co-transport with Na⁺ against a concentration gradient [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
In one population, 1 in 2 500 babies is born with cystic fibrosis, a recessive condition.

Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to calculate the proportion of babies who are carriers. (3)

In a population of snails, 16 % have the recessive pale shell (pp).

Calculate the percentage of snails that are heterozygous. (3)
State three conditions that must be met for the Hardy-Weinberg equation to give accurate predictions. (3)
hints: Think about population size and mating.
questions.solution:
Large population [B1]
Random mating [B1]
No mutation [B1]
No migration / gene flow in or out [B1]
No natural selection (all genotypes equally likely to survive and reproduce) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
A section of DNA has 200 base pairs. 30 % of the base pairs are A–T and 70 % are C–G.

Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands. (1)
hints: A–T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds; C–G pairs have 3.

questions.prompt:
In a DNA molecule, 22 % of the bases are thymine.

Calculate the percentage of bases that are guanine. (1)
Explain why a DNA molecule with a high proportion of C–G base pairs needs a higher temperature to separate its strands. (1)
hints: Count the hydrogen bonds per pair.
More bonds need more energy to break.
questions.solution: C–G pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds (A–T have 2), so more energy is needed to break them [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why different mutations in the CFTR gene can cause symptoms of different severity. (2)
hints: Different mutations change the protein in different ways.
questions.solution:
Different mutations change the amino acid sequence in different places / to different extents [B1]
So the CFTR protein may be partly functional, non-functional or not made / not reach the membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with cystic fibrosis have thick, sticky mucus in their airways. (2)
hints: CFTR is a chloride ion channel.
Link ions to water movement by osmosis.
questions.solution:
Faulty CFTR, so chloride ions are not moved out of epithelial cells into the mucus [B1]
Less water leaves the cells by osmosis, so mucus is not diluted / stays thick [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with cystic fibrosis often have problems digesting food. (2)
hints: The pancreatic duct can be blocked by mucus.
What do the enzymes from the pancreas do?
questions.solution:
Thick mucus blocks the pancreatic duct, so less enzyme reaches the small intestine [B1]
So less digestion / absorption of food (and pancreatic damage) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the primary structure of a protein. (2)
questions.solution:
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide [B1]
Joined by peptide bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the secondary structure of a protein. (2)
questions.solution:
Folding of the polypeptide into α-helices or β-pleated sheets [B1]
Held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two types of bond that hold the tertiary structure of a protein in shape. (2)
hints: One is covalent, between sulfur atoms.
questions.solution: Any two of: disulfide bridges, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions [B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
Porphyria is caused by a mutation in a gene for an enzyme used to make haem.

Explain why this mutation may stop the enzyme functioning correctly. (4)
hints: Base sequence → amino acid sequence → shape.
questions.solution:
The mutation changes the base sequence of the gene [B1]
So the mRNA codons and amino acid sequence change [B1]
So the bonds between R groups and the tertiary structure change [B1]
The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits [B1]
Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes / no haem made [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a frameshift mutation usually has a greater effect on a protein than a substitution mutation. (4)
hints: What does insertion or deletion do to the reading frame?
questions.solution:
Frameshift is caused by insertion or deletion of a base [B1]
Changes every codon after the mutation [B1]
So many amino acids are changed / premature stop codon [B1]
A substitution changes only one codon, which may even code for the same amino acid [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a mutation in a gene for a membrane channel protein could cause a disease. (4)
hints: What would happen to ion movement?
questions.solution:
Base sequence changes so the amino acid sequence changes [B1]
Protein folds differently / tertiary structure changes [B1]
Channel may not open / be non-functional / not inserted in membrane [B1]
Ions cannot cross the membrane, affecting water movement or cell function (e.g. CF) [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
Porphyria is caused by a dominant allele, P. A woman with porphyria (Pp) has children with an unaffected man (pp).

What is the probability that their child will have porphyria? (1)
hints: The man can only pass on p.
Half the woman's gametes carry P.

questions.prompt:
Two people who both have a dominant genetic disorder have an unaffected child.

State the genotypes of the parents. (1)
hints: The child must be homozygous recessive.
Each parent passed on a recessive allele.
questions.solution: Both parents are heterozygous (e.g. Pp × Pp) [B1]

questions.prompt: A heterozygous couple, both with a dominant condition, plan a son. What is the probability that he will have the condition? (1)
hints: Sex doesn't matter for an autosomal condition.

questions.prompt:
Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can bind to a specific mRNA and stop it being translated.

Deduce how siRNA could be used to prevent the symptoms of a disease caused by a dominant allele. (4)
hints: The siRNA must be complementary to something.
Which protein would no longer be made?
questions.solution:
siRNA has a base sequence complementary to the mRNA from the faulty (dominant) allele [B1]
It binds to this mRNA by complementary base pairing [B1]
The mRNA is broken down / cannot attach to ribosomes [B1]
So the faulty protein is not made, while the normal allele is still expressed [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a treatment using siRNA would need to be repeated, while gene therapy of stem cells might not. (4)
hints: siRNA is broken down in cells.
questions.solution:
siRNA is eventually broken down by enzymes [B1]
It does not change the DNA, so the faulty gene is still transcribed [B1]
Gene therapy of stem cells inserts the allele into the genome [B1]
Stem cells divide, passing the allele to new cells, so the effect lasts [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Compare somatic cell gene therapy and germ line gene therapy. (4)
questions.solution:
Somatic therapy alters body cells; germ line alters gametes or embryos [B1]
Somatic changes are not inherited; germ line changes are passed to offspring [B1]
Somatic therapy needs repeating as cells are replaced [B1]
Germ line therapy raises more ethical concerns and is currently illegal in humans in the UK [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why placing beetroot in alcohol increases the release of red pigment (betalain) from the cells. (3)
hints: What is the membrane made of?
questions.solution:
Alcohol dissolves the phospholipids in membranes [B1]
Membranes (tonoplast and cell surface) become more permeable / damaged [B1]
Betalain leaks out of the vacuole and cell [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why high temperatures increase the permeability of beetroot cell membranes. (3)
questions.solution:
Phospholipids gain kinetic energy and move more, making gaps [B1]
Membrane proteins denature, leaving holes [B1]
So betalain leaks out more easily [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a colorimeter can be used to measure the amount of pigment released from beetroot discs. (3)
questions.solution:
Zero / calibrate the colorimeter with distilled water [B1]
Use a suitable (blue-green) filter / wavelength absorbed by the pigment [B1]
Measure absorbance of the solution — higher absorbance means more pigment released [B1]

questions.prompt:
When two yellow mice were crossed, some offspring were non-yellow. When two non-yellow mice were crossed, all offspring were non-yellow.

Explain which allele is recessive. (2)
hints: Can two parents with the same phenotype produce a different one?
The hidden allele must be recessive.
questions.solution:
Non-yellow is recessive [B1]
Two yellow parents produced non-yellow offspring, so the parents carried a hidden allele (heterozygous) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a test cross can show whether a tall pea plant is homozygous or heterozygous. (2)
questions.solution:
Cross the tall plant with a homozygous recessive (short) plant [B1]
If any offspring are short, the tall plant is heterozygous; if all tall, homozygous [B1]

questions.prompt:
In snapdragons, red-flowered and white-flowered plants produce pink-flowered offspring.

Name this type of inheritance and explain the result. (2)
questions.solution:
Codominance [B1]
Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, giving an intermediate phenotype [B1]

questions.prompt: Two heterozygous yellow mice (Yy) produced 1600 offspring. Predict the numbers of yellow and non-yellow offspring using a 3 : 1 ratio. (2)
questions.solution:
Yellow = 1200 [B1]
Non-yellow = 400 [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a cross between two heterozygous yellow mice gives a 2 : 1 ratio of yellow to non-yellow, if the YY genotype is lethal. (2)
questions.solution:
YY embryos die, so only Yy and yy are born [B1]
Ratio of Yy : yy is 2 : 1 [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb) is crossed with aabb. Predict the ratio of phenotypes. (2)
questions.solution:
Gametes AB, Ab, aB, ab × ab [M1]
Ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 [A1]

questions.prompt:
From the cross of two yellow mice, 1064 offspring were yellow and 535 were non-yellow, rather than the 3 : 1 ratio predicted.

Explain the difference. (3)
questions.solution:
Actual ratio is about 2 : 1 [B1]
Suggests homozygous YY is lethal / embryos die before birth [B1]
So all yellow mice are heterozygous (Yy) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red–green colour blindness is much more common in men than in women. (3)
hints: How many X chromosomes do men have?
questions.solution:
The allele is recessive and carried on the X chromosome [B1]
Men have only one X, so one recessive allele causes colour blindness [B1]
Women need two recessive alleles; with one they are carriers [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a dihybrid test cross, the expected 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio was not seen. Most offspring had the parental combinations of characteristics.

Explain why. (3)
questions.solution:
The genes are linked / on the same chromosome [B1]
So they are usually inherited together [B1]
Recombinants only occur where crossing over happens between the loci, so are less common [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which structure is found in animal cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Amyloplast
B  Chloroplast
C  Mesosome
D  Ribosome (1)
hints: Which of these is in every eukaryotic cell?
questions.solution: D — ribosome. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Amyloplast
B  Golgi apparatus
C  Mesosome
D  Lysosome (1)
questions.solution: A — amyloplast. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which structure is found in both plant and animal cells?

Choose one answer.

A  Cellulose cell wall
B  Pili
C  Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
D  Plasmodesmata (1)
hints: Which organelle makes lipids in all eukaryotes?
questions.solution: C — smooth endoplasmic reticulum. [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an electron micrograph at a magnification of ×25 000, a mitochondrion measures 45 mm long.

Calculate its actual length in µm. (2)

A nucleus has an actual diameter of 8 µm. In a micrograph it measures 40 mm.

Calculate the magnification of the micrograph. (2)
hints: Convert both lengths to the same unit first.

questions.prompt: A bacterium is 2.5 µm long. Calculate how long it would appear in a drawing at a magnification of ×12 000. Give your answer in mm. (2)
Devise an investigation to test whether the percentage of cells in mitosis decreases with distance from the root tip. (5)
hints: How will you make a root tip squash and stain chromosomes?
How will you sample and calculate the mitotic index?
questions.solution:
Cut root tip (e.g. garlic) and place in hydrochloric acid (warm) to separate cells / break down the middle lamella [B1]
Stain with toluidine blue / acetic orcein to show chromosomes [B1]
Squash under a coverslip to make a single layer of cells [B1]
Count cells in mitosis and total cells in fields of view at measured distances from the tip (using a graticule) [B1]
Calculate mitotic index (cells in mitosis ÷ total cells) at each distance [B1]
Repeat with several roots and use a Spearman's rank test [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how to prepare and stain a root tip squash to observe stages of mitosis. Explain the reason for each step. (5)
hints: Why do you need a thin layer of cells?
questions.solution:
Cut the tip (1–2 cm) because this is where cells divide (meristem) [B1]
Place in warm hydrochloric acid to break down the middle lamella / separate cells / stop mitosis [B1]
Rinse to remove acid [B1]
Stain with toluidine blue / orcein to make chromosomes visible [B1]
Squash gently under a coverslip to make a single layer of cells so light passes through [B1]
View under high power to identify stages [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt:
In a root tip squash, a student counted 400 cells. 36 were in prophase, 8 in metaphase, 4 in anaphase and 2 in telophase. The cell cycle lasts 22 hours.

Calculate the mitotic index and estimate how long mitosis lasts. (5)
hints: Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total cells.
The proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to its time.
questions.solution:
Cells in mitosis = 36 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 50 [M1]
Mitotic index = 50 ÷ 400 = 0.125 [A1]
Time in mitosis = 0.125 × 22 h [M1]
= 2.75 h (2 h 45 min) [A1]
Assumes cells are dividing randomly / not synchronised [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of bond that holds neighbouring cellulose molecules together in a microfibril. (1)
hints: The bonds form between OH groups.
Many weak bonds add up to great strength.
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the substance that cements cellulose microfibrils together in the plant cell wall matrix. (1)
hints: It is also found in the middle lamella.
It is a polysaccharide used in jam making.
questions.solution: Pectin (or hemicellulose) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the substance deposited in the walls of xylem vessels that makes them waterproof and strong. (1)
questions.solution: Lignin [B1]

questions.prompt:
Cells in one region of a root are genetically identical, yet some become phloem sieve tube elements and others become companion cells.

Explain how this happens. (3)
hints: All cells have the same genes, but…
questions.solution:
Cells are exposed to different signals / chemical stimuli [B1]
Different genes are switched on (expressed) or off [B1]
Via transcription factors binding to promoters / mRNA transcribed from active genes only [B1]
Different proteins made, which change the structure and function of the cell [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why embryonic stem cells could be used to treat a wider range of diseases than adult stem cells. (3)
hints: How many cell types can each form?
questions.solution:
Embryonic stem cells are totipotent / pluripotent [B1]
Can differentiate into any / almost any cell type [B1]
Adult stem cells are multipotent, only forming a few related cell types [B1]
So embryonic cells could replace many different damaged tissues [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how DNA methylation and histone modification can affect gene expression. (3)
hints: These change how tightly DNA is packed.
Can RNA polymerase reach the gene?
questions.solution:
Methyl groups added to DNA (cytosine) prevent transcription factors / RNA polymerase binding [B1]
Acetylation of histones loosens chromatin so genes can be transcribed [B1]
Deacetylation / methylation of histones packs chromatin tightly, so genes are switched off [B1]
These changes do not alter the base sequence and can be inherited by daughter cells [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Plasmodium, the parasite that causes malaria, is a single-celled organism.

Give two structures that would show it is eukaryotic, and explain why. (2)
hints: Think about the nucleus and organelles.
questions.solution:
Nucleus with nuclear envelope — prokaryotes have free DNA [B1]
Membrane-bound organelles, e.g. mitochondria / ER / Golgi — absent from prokaryotes [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between the ribosomes and DNA of a prokaryotic cell and those of a eukaryotic cell. (2)
questions.solution:
Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller (70S) than eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S) [B1]
Prokaryotic DNA is circular and not associated with histones; eukaryotic DNA is linear with histones [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why viruses are not considered to be cells. (2)
questions.solution:
No cytoplasm / organelles / cell membrane [B1]
Can only replicate inside a host cell / no metabolism of their own [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of the organelles involved in folding, modifying and secreting a protein after it has been translated. (5)
questions.solution:
Ribosomes on rough ER make the polypeptide, which enters the ER [B1]
Polypeptide folds into its tertiary structure in the rough ER [B1]
Transported to the Golgi apparatus in vesicles [B1]
Golgi modifies the protein, e.g. adds carbohydrate (glycoproteins) [B1]
Golgi packages the protein into vesicles [B1]
Vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the protein by exocytosis [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt:
Pancreatic cells secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes.

Explain how the ultrastructure of these cells is adapted to this function. (5)
hints: Which organelles make, modify and package proteins?
Where does the energy come from?
questions.solution:
Large nucleus / nucleolus to make mRNA and ribosomes [B1]
Lots of rough ER with ribosomes to synthesise proteins [B1]
Large Golgi apparatus to modify and package enzymes [B1]
Many secretory vesicles [B1]
Many mitochondria to provide ATP for synthesis and exocytosis [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how a polypeptide is made from the base sequence of a gene. (5)
questions.solution:
DNA unwinds; RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides complementary to the template strand [B1]
mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore [B1]
mRNA attaches to a ribosome [B1]
tRNA with complementary anticodons bring specific amino acids to codons [B1]
Peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids [B1]
Ribosome moves along until a stop codon [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a fertilised egg contains only mitochondria from the mother. (2)
questions.solution:
Sperm mitochondria are in the midpiece, which does not enter the egg (only the nucleus / head enters) [B1]
Any sperm mitochondria that enter are destroyed; the egg has many mitochondria in its cytoplasm [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the acrosome reaction during fertilisation in mammals. (2)
questions.solution:
Acrosome fuses with the sperm cell membrane, releasing digestive enzymes [B1]
Enzymes digest the zona pellucida so the sperm can reach the egg membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how polyspermy is prevented after a sperm fuses with an egg. (2)
hints: What happens to the zona pellucida?
questions.solution:
Cortical granules release their contents by exocytosis (cortical reaction) [B1]
Zona pellucida hardens, so no other sperm can enter [B1]

questions.prompt:
In mitochondrial donation, the nucleus of a fertilised egg from a woman with faulty mitochondria is transferred into a donor egg that has had its nucleus removed.

Explain why the embryo does not develop the mitochondrial disease. (2)
questions.solution:
The faulty genes are in mitochondrial DNA [B1]
The embryo's mitochondria come from the donor egg, which has healthy mitochondria [B1]

questions.prompt:
A mother has a disease caused by faulty mitochondrial DNA. The father does not.

Explain why all of their children inherit the faulty mitochondria. (2)
hints: Mitochondrial DNA is not in the nucleus.
questions.solution:
Mitochondria are inherited only from the mother, through the egg cytoplasm [B1]
So all her children receive faulty mitochondrial DNA (though severity may vary) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a man with a mitochondrial disease cannot pass it on to his children. (2)
hints: Where do the zygote's mitochondria come from?
questions.solution:
Sperm mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote [B1]
All mitochondria come from the egg / mother [B1]

questions.prompt: Comment on the inheritance of characteristics in a child produced by mitochondrial donation. (3)
questions.solution:
Nuclear DNA comes from the mother and father, so almost all characteristics come from them [B1]
Mitochondrial DNA (a small number of genes) comes from the donor [B1]
So the child has DNA from three people [B1]
Mitochondrial genes mainly affect respiration, not appearance [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss ethical issues of using mitochondrial donation to prevent disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Benefit: prevents a serious inherited disease [B1]
Concern: genetic change is passed to future generations / long-term effects unknown [B1]
Concern: embryos may be destroyed / 'designer babies' slippery slope [B1]
Concern: identity issues with three genetic parents [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
A sheep was cloned by transferring the nucleus of a udder cell into an enucleated egg cell.

Explain why the clone is not 100 % genetically identical to the udder cell donor. (3)
hints: Not all DNA is in the nucleus.
questions.solution:
Nuclear DNA is identical to the donor [B1]
But mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg cell donor [B1]
Epigenetic marks may differ / mutations may arise [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the mass of nuclear DNA is the same in a sperm cell and an egg cell of the same species. (1)
hints: Each has one set of chromosomes.
questions.solution: Both are haploid / contain one copy of each chromosome (23 in humans) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one structural difference between a human sperm cell and an egg cell. (1)
questions.solution: Sperm is small with a flagellum / acrosome; egg is large with lots of cytoplasm / zona pellucida [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one way in which meiosis produces genetic variation. (1)
questions.solution: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes / independent assortment of chromosomes [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of a sperm cell that contains enzymes for respiration. (1)
questions.solution: Midpiece (middle piece) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the midpiece of a sperm cell contains many mitochondria. (1)
questions.solution: To produce ATP by aerobic respiration for movement of the flagellum [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of the acrosome. (1)
hints: It helps the sperm get into the egg.
questions.solution: Releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida [B1]

questions.prompt:
People adapted to life at high altitude have more red blood cells.

Explain how a stem cell in the bone marrow gives rise to red blood cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Stem cells divide by mitosis [B1]
Some daughter cells differentiate as certain genes are switched on [B1]
Producing proteins such as haemoglobin [B1]
Cells lose their nucleus and most organelles to make room for haemoglobin / biconcave shape [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how stem cells could be used to treat a disease, and one difficulty with this treatment. (4)
questions.solution:
Stem cells are stimulated to differentiate into the required cell type [B1]
Transplanted into the patient to replace damaged cells (e.g. pancreatic β cells) [B1]
Difficulty: may be rejected by the immune system [B1]
Difficulty: may divide uncontrollably / form tumours; ethical issues with embryonic cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) are made and why they reduce ethical concerns. (4)
questions.solution:
Adult (somatic) cells are taken from the patient [B1]
Genes for transcription factors are introduced to switch on genes for pluripotency [B1]
Cells become pluripotent and can be differentiated into many cell types [B1]
No embryos are destroyed; patient's own cells, so less risk of rejection [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the DNA found in a prokaryotic cell. (1)
questions.solution: A single circular (double-stranded) chromosome and small circular plasmids, not associated with histones [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of plasmids in bacteria. (1)
questions.solution: Carry extra genes such as antibiotic resistance genes, which can be passed between bacteria [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of pili in bacteria. (1)
questions.solution: Attach to surfaces / other bacteria (e.g. for transfer of plasmids) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two organelles, other than the Golgi apparatus and rough ER, that are surrounded by a single membrane. (1)
questions.solution: Two of: lysosome, smooth ER, vesicle, (plant) vacuole [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two organelles surrounded by a double membrane. (1)
questions.solution: Two of: nucleus, mitochondrion, chloroplast [B1]

questions.prompt: Name an organelle not surrounded by any membrane. (1)
hints: Or a pair of these makes spindles.
questions.solution: Ribosome (or centriole) [B1]

questions.prompt:
In liver cells, Golgi apparatus makes up 7 % and rough ER 35 % of the total membrane. In pancreas cells the figures are 10 % and 60 %.

Explain these differences. (5)
hints: Which cells secrete large amounts of protein?
Liver cells do many other jobs.
questions.solution:
Pancreas cells secrete large amounts of protein (digestive enzymes) [B1]
So need more rough ER for protein synthesis [B1]
And more Golgi for modifying and packaging proteins into vesicles [B1]
Liver cells have many other roles needing other organelles, e.g. smooth ER for lipid metabolism / detoxification [B1]
Liver cells have more mitochondria / other membranes, so a smaller proportion is rough ER and Golgi [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why muscle cells have many mitochondria, while plasma cells have a lot of rough ER. (5)
hints: What does each cell make or do most?
questions.solution:
Muscle cells contract, which needs a lot of ATP [B1]
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration / produce ATP [B1]
Plasma cells secrete large amounts of antibodies [B1]
Antibodies are proteins made on ribosomes on rough ER [B1]
Specialisation results from different genes being expressed [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how cell fractionation could be used to obtain a sample of mitochondria from liver tissue. (5)
questions.solution:
Homogenise tissue in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution [B1]
Cold reduces enzyme activity; isotonic prevents organelles bursting; buffer stops proteins denaturing [B1]
Filter to remove debris [B1]
Centrifuge at low speed; nuclei form the pellet [B1]
Centrifuge the supernatant at higher speed; mitochondria form the next pellet [B1]

questions.prompt:
A human gene is 74 775 base pairs long, but the protein it codes for has only 132 amino acids.

Explain the differences between the gene and the mRNA it produces. (6)
hints: How many bases code for 132 amino acids?
questions.solution:
132 amino acids need only 396 bases (plus a stop codon) [B1]
The gene contains introns (non-coding) and exons [B1]
The whole gene is transcribed into pre-mRNA [B1]
Introns are removed by splicing [B1]
mRNA is single-stranded, contains uracil not thymine, ribose not deoxyribose [B1]
mRNA also has non-coding regions at each end / alternative splicing of exons [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Humans have about 20 000 genes but make over 100 000 different proteins.

Explain how this is possible. (6)
hints: One gene can give several mRNAs.
questions.solution:
Genes contain exons separated by introns [B1]
Pre-mRNA is spliced to remove introns [B1]
Exons can be joined in different combinations (alternative splicing) [B1]
So different mRNAs are made from one gene [B1]
Each mRNA codes for a different polypeptide / protein [B1]
Proteins can also be modified after translation (e.g. by the Golgi) [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the lac operon is switched on in E. coli when lactose is present. (6)
questions.solution:
Regulator gene codes for a repressor protein [B1]
Without lactose, the repressor binds to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase [B1]
Lactose binds to the repressor, changing its shape [B1]
Repressor can no longer bind to the operator [B1]
RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and transcribes the structural genes [B1]
Producing β-galactosidase to break down lactose [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of the term species. (1)
hints: The offspring must be able to breed too.
questions.solution: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring [B1]

questions.prompt:
A horse and a donkey can breed to produce a mule, but mules are sterile.

Explain why horses and donkeys are classed as separate species. (1)
hints: Use the definition of a species.
questions.solution: The offspring (mules) are not fertile, so horses and donkeys cannot produce fertile offspring together [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of the term niche. (1)
hints: It is more than just where an organism lives.
Think about how it interacts with its environment.
questions.solution: The role of an organism in its habitat / how it uses biotic and abiotic resources and interacts with other organisms [B1]

questions.prompt:
The common grass snake is olive green with a yellow collar. The barred grass snake is grey with black bars. They share a common ancestor.

Explain how these two species could have arisen from a common ancestor. (4)
hints: What stops the two groups interbreeding?
questions.solution:
Mutations produced variation in colour / markings [B1]
Snakes with better camouflage in their habitat survived and reproduced / passed on alleles [B1]
Different allele frequencies built up in the two populations [B1]
Populations became reproductively isolated (e.g. geographical / behavioural) [B1]
Eventually they could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
Two species of cichlid fish live in the same lake. One feeds on algae on rocks and the other feeds on insects in open water. Females of each species only mate with males of a particular colour.

Explain how these species could have arisen by sympatric speciation. (4)
hints: Sympatric means in the same place — so no geographical barrier.
Link mate choice to reproductive isolation.
questions.solution:
Mutation gave variation in feeding / colour within one population [B1]
Different feeding niches favoured different phenotypes (selection pressure) [B1]
Females chose mates of a particular colour so the groups did not interbreed (behavioural isolation) [B1]
Gene flow stopped and allele frequencies diverged [B1]
Until the groups could no longer produce fertile offspring together [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
A population of mice was split into two when a new river formed. After many thousands of years the two populations can no longer interbreed.

Explain how this happened. (4)
hints: Each side may have had different selection pressures.
questions.solution:
The river is a geographical barrier, so no gene flow between the populations [B1]
Different mutations arose in each population [B1]
Different environments / selection pressures on each side [B1]
So different allele frequencies built up by natural selection (and genetic drift) [B1]
Leading to reproductive isolation / they can no longer produce fertile offspring [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
Leaf rust is a fungal disease of wheat that spreads more easily when the air is warm and humid.

Discuss the possible impact of climate change on the yield of wheat crops. (4)
hints: Climate change alters more than temperature.
Consider effects that could increase or decrease yield.
questions.solution:
Climate change will alter temperature, rainfall and humidity in different regions [B1]
Warmer, more humid conditions could help leaf rust grow and spread, reducing yield [B1]
Drier conditions / drought might limit the spread of rust [B1]
Higher temperature and CO₂ may increase photosynthesis and yield (up to a point) [B1]
Drought or extreme temperatures may reduce yield regardless of disease [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how climate change may affect the distribution of a butterfly species that feeds only on one type of plant. (4)
hints: Butterflies may move, but can their food plant move as fast?
Think about temperature ranges and breeding seasons.
questions.solution:
Temperature rises may make new areas (further north / higher altitude) suitable [B1]
Butterfly range may shift towards the poles / uphill [B1]
But it depends on the food plant also being able to grow there [B1]
Plant may spread more slowly than the butterfly / habitat may be fragmented [B1]
Timing mismatch between butterfly emergence and plant growth could reduce numbers [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, which develop faster at higher temperatures. Discuss how climate change could affect the number of people infected with malaria. (4)
hints: Consider where mosquitoes could survive in a warmer world.
questions.solution:
Higher temperatures speed up mosquito development / reproduction [B1]
Mosquitoes could survive in new areas (higher altitudes / latitudes) [B1]
So more people exposed, possibly with no immunity [B1]
More rainfall creates more breeding sites (standing water) [B1]
But drought / very high temperatures could reduce mosquito numbers in some areas [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why emissions of greenhouse gases from human activities are causing the climate to change. (3)
hints: Name an activity and a gas.
What do greenhouse gases do to infrared radiation?
questions.solution:
Named human activity, e.g. burning fossil fuels / deforestation / cattle farming / landfill [B1]
Increases concentration of a named gas (CO₂ / methane) [B1]
More infrared radiation (heat) from the Earth is absorbed and re-radiated / trapped [B1]
So the mean global temperature rises [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how deforestation contributes to an increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide. (3)
hints: Two effects: less uptake and more release.
questions.solution:
Fewer trees, so less photosynthesis to remove CO₂ [B1]
Trees are often burned, releasing CO₂ [B1]
Decomposition of wood / soil by microorganisms releases CO₂ through respiration [B1]
Carbon stored for many years in trees is released [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe three types of evidence that the Earth's climate is changing. (3)
hints: Think about temperatures, ice and living things.
Some evidence comes from the past (ice cores, pollen).
questions.solution:
Temperature records show a rise in mean global temperature [B1]
Dendrochronology (tree rings) / peat bog pollen shows past climate change [B1]
Ice cores show CO₂ concentration correlates with temperature [B1]
Changes in timing of seasonal events / species ranges / ice cover [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Pteropods are tiny sea snails with calcium carbonate shells, eaten by many fish. In 2011, 53 % of pteropods sampled off one coast had damaged shells. Data from three ocean sites show that, from 1980 to 2020, dissolved CO₂ rose steadily and the pH of seawater fell.

Use this information to discuss the likely effect of carbon dioxide emissions on fish populations that feed on pteropods. (6)
hints: Build a chain: CO₂ → pH → shells → pteropods → fish.
Consider a short-term effect as well as a long-term one.
questions.solution:
Human CO₂ emissions increase atmospheric CO₂, which dissolves in seawater [B1]
Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH (ocean acidification) [B1]
Lower pH dissolves / damages calcium carbonate shells (53 % damaged) [B1]
Pteropods die or grow / reproduce less, so their population falls [B1]
Less food for fish, so fish populations decline / fish change prey [B1]
Possible short-term rise in fish as damaged pteropods are easier to catch; data are correlational and from a few sites only [B1]
Level-marked: a full answer links all steps in a logical chain (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Coral reefs contain algae that photosynthesise and provide corals with sugars. When sea temperature rises by 1–2 °C above normal, corals expel their algae and turn white (bleaching). Reefs provide food and shelter for about a quarter of all marine fish species.

Discuss the likely impact of rising sea temperatures on fish biodiversity. (6)
hints: Follow the chain from temperature to algae to coral to fish.
Consider acidification and recovery as well.
questions.solution:
Higher CO₂ emissions raise sea temperature [B1]
Corals expel algae, so lose their sugar supply [B1]
Repeated bleaching causes corals to die; reef structure breaks down [B1]
Loss of habitat, shelter and food for fish [B1]
So fish population sizes and species richness / biodiversity fall [B1]
Ocean acidification also weakens coral skeletons; some corals may recover if temperatures return to normal [B1]
Level-marked: a full answer links all steps in a logical chain (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
In the Arctic, the date when sea ice melts each spring has moved earlier by about 3 weeks since 1980. Algae that grow under the ice are eaten by krill, which are eaten by Arctic cod, which are eaten by seals.

Discuss how continued climate change could affect the seal population. (6)
hints: What does earlier melting do to the algae?
Follow the food chain step by step.
questions.solution:
Climate change raises temperatures, causing earlier and greater ice melt [B1]
Less sea ice means less habitat for under-ice algae [B1]
So less food for krill; krill numbers fall [B1]
Fewer krill means less food for Arctic cod [B1]
So less food for seals, and seals also lose ice for breeding / resting, so numbers fall [B1]
Seals may switch to other prey, or species from further south may move in [B1]
Level-marked: a full answer links all steps in a logical chain (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
One serving of beef produces about 7 kg of greenhouse gas emissions; one serving of beans produces about 0.5 kg.

Explain why a diet based on plant protein produces lower emissions than a diet based on animal protein. (3)
hints: Think about energy loss between trophic levels.
questions.solution:
Energy is lost at each trophic level, so far more crops are needed to feed animals than to feed people directly [B1]
More land needed / more fertiliser, machinery, transport [B1]
Cattle produce methane from digestion [B1]
Methane is a potent greenhouse gas [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why beef farmed on land cleared from rainforest produces more greenhouse gas emissions than beef grazed on natural grassland. (3)
hints: What is lost when forest is removed?
questions.solution:
Trees are burned or decompose, releasing CO₂ [B1]
Loss of trees means less photosynthesis / less CO₂ removed [B1]
Carbon stored in soil is released when it is disturbed [B1]
Grassland already exists, so no extra loss of carbon sink [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how planting a forest on farmland could help reduce the rate of climate change. (3)
questions.solution:
Growing trees take up CO₂ for photosynthesis [B1]
Carbon is stored in wood / biomass for many years (carbon sink) [B1]
Rate of photosynthesis exceeds respiration while trees are growing [B1]
Less CO₂ in the atmosphere, so less greenhouse effect [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: State how the age of a layer of peat can be found. (1)
questions.solution: Radiocarbon dating / carbon-14 dating (deeper layers are older) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how pollen grains preserved in peat can provide evidence of past climate. (1)
hints: Each plant species has distinctive pollen.
questions.solution: Pollen identifies which plant species were present, and each species grows in particular climate conditions [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tree rings provide evidence of past climate (dendrochronology). (1)
hints: Rings are wider in some years.
questions.solution: Wide rings form in warm / wet years and narrow rings in cold / dry years [B1]

questions.prompt:
Biodiversity can be measured as genetic diversity. What is genetic diversity?

Choose one answer.

A  The number of species in a habitat
B  The number of different alleles in a population
C  The number of individuals in a population
D  The number of homozygotes in a population (1)
questions.solution: B — the number of different alleles in a population. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of species richness. (1)
questions.solution: The number of different species in a habitat [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of an endemic species. (1)
hints: It is found in only one place.
questions.solution: A species found naturally in only one geographic area [B1]

questions.prompt:
Biodiversity hotspots contain at least 1500 endemic plant species and have lost at least 70 % of their natural vegetation.

Explain why protecting these hotspots has a large effect on global biodiversity. (2)
hints: These areas are already under threat.
questions.solution:
They contain many endemic species found nowhere else, so their extinction would reduce global biodiversity [B1]
They are under high threat, so protection prevents many extinctions for relatively little land / cost [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two roles of zoos in conserving endangered species. (2)
questions.solution:
Captive breeding programmes, with stud books to maintain genetic diversity, and reintroduction [B1]
Education / research / raising money for conservation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of seed banks in conservation. (2)
hints: Seeds can be stored for a long time.
questions.solution:
Seeds are dried and stored at low temperature, so they remain viable for many years [B1]
Conserves genetic diversity; plants can be grown and reintroduced if wild populations are lost [B1]

questions.prompt:
A population of deer in Finland was founded from a few animals introduced from North America. The Finnish deer have fewer alleles per gene than North American deer.

Explain this difference. (3)
hints: How many alleles did the founders carry?
What can happen in small populations?
questions.solution:
The founders carried only a small proportion of the alleles in the original population (founder effect) [B1]
Some alleles were lost by chance / genetic drift in the small population [B1]
Little gene flow from other populations [B1]
So lower genetic diversity / allele richness [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why genetic drift has a greater effect in small populations than in large ones. (3)
hints: Chance events matter more when numbers are small.
questions.solution:
Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequency [B1]
In a small population, chance events (which individuals breed) have a large effect on frequencies [B1]
Alleles can be lost or become fixed quickly [B1]
In large populations chance effects average out [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Cheetah populations went through a severe bottleneck about 10 000 years ago. Explain why cheetahs today are at risk from disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Population fell to a few individuals, so many alleles were lost [B1]
Low genetic diversity / many homozygotes [B1]
If a new disease appears, few or none may have alleles for resistance [B1]
So the whole population could be affected [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
The heterozygosity index of a deer population in Finland is 0.69 and in North America is 0.74.

Explain which population is more likely to adapt to climate change. (4)
questions.solution:
North American population, because it has the higher heterozygosity index [B1]
So greater genetic diversity / more alleles [B1]
More likely that some individuals have alleles that are advantageous in the new conditions [B1]
These survive and reproduce, so allele frequencies change / population adapts [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a sample of 50 animals, 32 were heterozygous at a particular gene locus.

Calculate the heterozygosity index and explain what a low value would show. (4)
hints: H = number of heterozygotes ÷ number of individuals.
questions.solution:
H = 32 ÷ 50 [M1]
= 0.64 [A1]
A low value shows low genetic diversity / many homozygotes [B1]
Suggesting inbreeding / a small or bottlenecked population [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how zoos try to maintain genetic diversity in small captive populations of endangered animals. (4)
questions.solution:
Keep stud books / records of ancestry [B1]
Avoid breeding closely related animals (inbreeding) [B1]
Exchange animals or sperm between zoos worldwide [B1]
Use IVF / artificial insemination / frozen gametes [B1]

questions.prompt:
Where in a chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?

Choose one answer.

A  Cristae
B  Matrix
C  Stroma
D  Thylakoid membranes (1)
hints: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll — where are the photosystems?
The stroma is where the Calvin cycle happens.
questions.solution:
D — thylakoid membranes (grana). [B1]
The photosystems and electron transport chain are embedded in the thylakoid membranes; the stroma is the site of the light-independent reactions.

questions.prompt:
Which of these are all products of the light-dependent reactions?

Choose one answer.

A  ATP, reduced NADP and carbon dioxide
B  ATP, glucose and oxygen
C  GP, ATP and oxygen
D  ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen (1)
hints: The light-dependent reactions make the energy and reducing power used in the Calvin cycle.
Which by-product comes from photolysis of water?
questions.solution:
D — ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen. [B1]
ATP and reduced NADP pass to the light-independent reactions; oxygen is released from photolysis of water.

questions.prompt:
Which molecule is the original source of the hydrogen used to reduce NADP in photosynthesis?

Choose one answer.

A  Glucose
B  Reduced NAD
C  Water
D  Carbon dioxide (1)
hints: Water is split by light energy into H⁺, electrons and oxygen.
questions.solution:
C — water. [B1]
Photolysis splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; the H⁺ and electrons reduce NADP.

questions.prompt:
Growers often burn paraffin inside commercial glasshouses to raise the carbon dioxide concentration of the air.

Explain how this can increase the growth of the crop plants. (3)
hints: What is CO₂ used for in the Calvin cycle?
questions.solution:
Carbon dioxide is a limiting factor for photosynthesis [B1]
More CO₂ is fixed by RuBisCO / combined with RuBP to form more GP / GALP [B1]
So more glucose / carbohydrate / organic molecules are made [B1]
Used for respiration or to make new cell material, so faster growth / cell division [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
A grower fits LED lamps in a lettuce glasshouse so the plants are lit for 18 hours a day instead of 12.

Explain why this can increase the yield of lettuce. (3)
hints: Which stage of photosynthesis depends directly on light?
Think about what longer light periods do to total carbohydrate made per day.
questions.solution:
Light is a limiting factor / photosynthesis can occur for longer each day [B1]
More ATP and reduced NADP are produced in the light-dependent reactions [B1]
So more GP is reduced to GALP / more carbohydrate is made in the Calvin cycle [B1]
More biomass / net primary productivity, so larger plants / higher yield [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
In winter a glasshouse is heated from 8 °C to 22 °C. The light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration are not changed.

Explain why the rate of growth of the plants increases. (3)
hints: Which part of photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes?
Think about kinetic energy and enzyme–substrate complexes.
questions.solution:
Temperature was a limiting factor [B1]
Enzymes of the Calvin cycle (e.g. RuBisCO) have more kinetic energy, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
So the light-independent reactions are faster / more CO₂ is fixed / more GALP made [B1]
More carbohydrate for respiration and growth / increased NPP [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Primary consumers in a river ecosystem took in 14 200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of energy. Of this, 4 700 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ was fixed as new biomass. All of the remaining energy was lost in respiration.

Calculate the energy lost in respiration. (1)
hints: Energy intake = energy in new biomass + energy lost.

questions.prompt:
The biomass of primary consumers in a pond was 5 200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and the biomass of secondary consumers was 468 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.

Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from primary to secondary consumers. Give your answer to one decimal place. (1)
hints: Efficiency = (energy at higher level ÷ energy at lower level) × 100.

questions.prompt:
An ecosystem receives 6 400 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of sunlight. The gross primary productivity of the producers is 96 000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.

Calculate the percentage of the light energy that is fixed by the producers. (1)
Explain why the gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is much lower than the light energy that falls on it. (3)
hints: Not all light reaches or is absorbed by chlorophyll.
Think about reflection, transmission and wavelength.
questions.solution:
Not all light falls on leaves / some hits bare ground or water [B1]
Some light is reflected from the leaf surface [B1]
Some light passes through the leaf / misses the chloroplasts [B1]
Some light is the wrong wavelength to be absorbed by chlorophyll [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the net primary productivity of a crop is always lower than its gross primary productivity. (3)
hints: What do plants use some of their glucose for?
questions.solution:
NPP = GPP minus respiratory losses [B1]
Plants use some of the carbohydrate they make in respiration [B1]
Energy released in respiration is used for metabolism / active transport and lost as heat [B1]
So this energy is not stored as new biomass [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Only about 10 % of the energy in primary consumers becomes biomass in secondary consumers.

Give three reasons why. (3)
hints: Not all of the prey is eaten or digested.
Where else does energy go in the consumer?
questions.solution:
Not all of the primary consumer is eaten (e.g. bones, fur) [B1]
Some is not digested / lost in faeces [B1]
Energy is lost in excretion (urine) [B1]
Energy is lost as heat from respiration / used in movement [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of the surrounding temperature on the rate at which a dead body decomposes. (3)
hints: Decomposition is carried out by microorganisms using enzymes.
questions.solution:
Higher temperature increases the rate of decomposition (and vice versa) [B1]
Enzymes of decomposers have more kinetic energy / more enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Decomposers / insects grow and reproduce faster [B1]
Very high temperatures may denature enzymes / at low temperatures enzymes are less active [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
A body found in a dry, sealed room had decomposed much more slowly than expected.

Suggest and explain why. (3)
hints: Think about water and access for insects.
questions.solution:
Little water / dry conditions reduce the activity of bacteria and fungi [B1]
Enzymes need water / hydrolysis reactions need water [B1]
Sealed room so insects (e.g. blowflies) could not reach the body to lay eggs [B1]
Low oxygen may slow aerobic decomposers [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the stage of decomposition alone gives only an approximate estimate of time of death. (3)
hints: What factors change how fast a body decomposes?
Think about where the body was and its size.
questions.solution:
Rate of decomposition depends on temperature [B1]
And on humidity / water availability / oxygen [B1]
Body mass / clothing / burial affects the rate [B1]
Access of insects and decomposers varies [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the changes that happen inside a body during the first few days after death. (3)
hints: Think about temperature, muscles and cells.
Which enzymes start digesting the body's own tissues?
questions.solution:
Body temperature falls (algor mortis) [B1]
Muscles become stiff (rigor mortis) as ATP runs out [B1]
Autolysis — the body's own enzymes break down cells [B1]
Bacteria cause putrefaction / gases build up, causing bloating / discolouration [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how rigor mortis develops after death and why it can be used to estimate time of death. (3)
hints: Rigor mortis follows a fairly predictable timeline.
questions.solution:
After death, respiration stops / no oxygen, so ATP is no longer made [B1]
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so muscles stay contracted / stiff [B1]
Rigor starts within a few hours and wears off after about 36 hours as proteins break down [B1]
So the extent of stiffness gives an approximate time since death [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how measuring body temperature can be used to estimate time of death, and why this method is only useful for the first 24 hours. (3)
hints: Body temperature falls at a roughly known rate.
What happens once it matches the surroundings?
questions.solution:
After death no respiration, so no heat generated / body cools [B1]
Cools at a roughly predictable rate (about 1–1.5 °C per hour) [B1]
After about 24 hours the body reaches the temperature of the surroundings [B1]
So no further change can be measured / rate affected by surroundings, clothing, body mass [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Plants need nitrate ions to make which of these?

Choose one answer.

B  Cellulose
C  Starch
D  Sucrose (1)
hints: Carbohydrates contain only C, H and O.
questions.solution: A — amino acids. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Plants need phosphate ions to make which of these?

Choose one answer.

A  Cellulose
B  Chlorophyll
C  Nucleic acids
D  Sucrose (1)
hints: Which molecule has a sugar–phosphate backbone?
questions.solution: C — nucleic acids. [B1]

questions.prompt: A plant grown without magnesium ions has yellow leaves. Explain why. (1)
questions.solution: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so less chlorophyll is made (chlorosis) [B1]

questions.prompt:
The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is lower than in the vacuoles of root hair cells.

Describe how root hair cells take up these ions. (3)
hints: The ions move against a concentration gradient.
questions.solution:
Active transport [B1]
Using carrier proteins in the cell surface membrane [B1]
Using ATP from respiration [B1]
Against the concentration gradient [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why waterlogged soils reduce the uptake of mineral ions by roots. (3)
hints: Which process needs oxygen and supplies ATP?
questions.solution:
Waterlogged soil has little oxygen [B1]
So less aerobic respiration in root cells [B1]
So less ATP available [B1]
For active transport of ions [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a root hair cell is adapted for taking up water and mineral ions. (3)
hints: Think about what active transport needs.
questions.solution:
Long extension gives a large surface area [B1]
Many carrier proteins in the membrane for active transport [B1]
Many mitochondria to provide ATP [B1]
Thin cell wall / short diffusion distance [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how waterlogged, acidic conditions in a peat bog prevent decomposition. (3)
hints: What does low pH do to enzymes?
questions.solution:
Waterlogging means little oxygen, so aerobic decomposers can't respire [B1]
Acidic conditions denature enzymes of decomposers [B1]
So few bacteria / fungi survive [B1]
Organic matter is not broken down, so it accumulates [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle. (3)
questions.solution:
Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on dead organic matter [B1]
Secrete enzymes to digest it extracellularly [B1]
Respire, releasing CO₂ into the atmosphere [B1]
Making carbon available for photosynthesis again [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why draining peat bogs for farmland increases atmospheric carbon dioxide. (3)
hints: What enters the peat when it is drained?
What happens to the stored carbon?
questions.solution:
Draining lets oxygen into the peat [B1]
Decomposers can now respire aerobically and break down the peat [B1]
Releasing stored carbon as CO₂ [B1]
Peat bog plants that absorbed CO₂ are lost [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
