The rate of photosynthesis of species A fell from 12.0 to 9.0 units when light was reduced. For species B it fell from 8.0 to 2.0 units.

Calculate the percentage change for each species and state which was affected most. (2)
questions.solution:
A: −25 %; B: −75 % [M1]
Species B was affected most [A1]

questions.prompt: Suggest two adaptations of plants that grow well in shade. (2)
hints: Think about leaf size and pigments.
How do they capture more light?
questions.solution:
Larger / thinner leaves to absorb more light [B1]
More chlorophyll / more photosystems / chlorophyll b; lower compensation point [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the compensation point of a plant. (2)
questions.solution:
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration [B1]
So there is no net gas exchange of CO₂ or O₂ [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why seedlings grown in higher light intensity have a faster growth rate. (4)
questions.solution:
More light energy absorbed, so faster light-dependent reactions [B1]
More ATP and reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle [B1]
More GALP / glucose made [B1]
Used to make cellulose, proteins etc. for new cells / more net primary productivity [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis. (4)
questions.solution:
CO₂ combines with RuBP, catalysed by RuBisCO [B1]
Forming two molecules of GP [B1]
GP is reduced to GALP using reduced NADP and ATP [B1]
Some GALP used to make glucose / other molecules; most regenerates RuBP using ATP [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. (4)
hints: Photosystems absorb light and excite electrons.
questions.solution:
Light excites electrons in chlorophyll in photosystems [B1]
Electrons pass along an electron transport chain, releasing energy to make ATP (photophosphorylation) [B1]
Photolysis of water replaces electrons, producing H⁺ and oxygen [B1]
Electrons and H⁺ reduce NADP [B1]

questions.prompt:
Two forms of grass snake look different. Scientists think they may be separate species.

Describe how DNA profiling could be used to show whether they are different species. (4)
hints: You need DNA fragments, then a way to separate them.
What would more differences in the band pattern show?
questions.solution:
Extract DNA from snakes of both forms [B1]
Amplify using PCR / cut into fragments with restriction enzymes [B1]
Separate the fragments by gel electrophoresis [B1]
Fragments separate by size / length [B1]
Many differences in band pattern indicate different species (similar patterns = same species) [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: A hair is found at a crime scene. Describe how a DNA profile can be produced from it and used to identify a suspect. (4)
hints: There is only a tiny amount of DNA at first.
Profiles are compared band by band.
questions.solution:
Extract DNA from the hair root / follicle cells [B1]
Amplify using PCR to make many copies [B1]
Cut with restriction enzymes / amplify short tandem repeats [B1]
Separate fragments by gel electrophoresis (and add probes / visualise bands) [B1]
Compare the band pattern with suspects' profiles — a match identifies the suspect [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments of different lengths. (4)
hints: Think about how easily fragments move through the gel.
questions.solution:
DNA samples placed in wells at the negative electrode end of the gel [B1]
DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups) [B1]
So it moves towards the positive electrode when a current is applied [B1]
Shorter fragments move faster / further through the gel [B1]
Bands made visible using a stain / fluorescent or radioactive probe [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
What does a bacteriostatic antibiotic do?

Choose one answer.

A  Destroys bacteria
B  Destroys viruses
C  Prevents bacteria from multiplying
D  Prevents bacteria becoming resistant (1)
questions.solution: C — prevents bacteria from multiplying. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one reason why antibiotics are not used to treat viral infections. (1)
hints: What do antibiotics target in bacteria?
questions.solution: Viruses have no cell wall / ribosomes / metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target (they replicate inside host cells) [B1]

questions.prompt: Penicillin is described as bactericidal. Give the meaning of bactericidal. (1)
questions.solution: It kills bacteria (e.g. by weakening the cell wall so the cell bursts) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three practices hospitals use to reduce hospital-acquired infections. (3)
hints: Think about hands, clothing and patients.
questions.solution:
Hand washing / alcohol gel stations for staff and visitors [B1]
Staff 'bare below the elbows' — no ties, watches or long sleeves [B1]
Screening new patients and isolating those with resistant bacteria (e.g. MRSA) [B1]
Thorough cleaning / disinfecting of surfaces and equipment / disposable equipment [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA become common in hospitals. (3)
hints: Why do hospitals give these bacteria an advantage?
questions.solution:
A mutation gives some bacteria resistance [B1]
Antibiotics are widely used in hospitals, so non-resistant bacteria are killed [B1]
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the allele (or transfer plasmids) [B1]
Many vulnerable patients / close contact spreads them [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Doctors are advised not to prescribe antibiotics for minor infections and to tell patients to finish the course. Explain how these rules reduce the development of antibiotic resistance. (3)
hints: Fewer antibiotics means less selection pressure.
What happens to partly resistant bacteria if a course is stopped early?
questions.solution:
Less use of antibiotics means less selection pressure for resistant bacteria [B1]
Finishing the course kills all the bacteria [B1]
Stopping early lets the more resistant bacteria survive and reproduce [B1]
Resistant alleles become less common in the population [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
The number of measles cases in a country fell from 1855 in one year to 135 the next year.

Calculate the percentage change to 3 significant figures. (2)

Vaccination rates in a region rose from 82 % to 95 % over five years.

Calculate the percentage increase in the vaccination rate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2)

Cases of a disease rose from 240 to 1020.

Calculate the percentage increase. (2)

In one country, the measles vaccination rate rose sharply in 2013, but measles cases did not fall to low levels until 2015.

Explain why an increase in vaccination rate takes time to reduce the number of cases. (4)
questions.solution:
It takes time for the immune response to produce memory cells after vaccination [B1]
Some children need two doses / vaccines are given at a particular age, so not everyone is protected at once [B1]
Herd immunity requires a high proportion (about 95 %) of the population to be immune [B1]
Until then, the virus can still spread to unvaccinated people [B1]
Infected people already incubating the virus still develop measles [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated. (4)
questions.solution:
A large proportion of the population is immune [B1]
So the pathogen is less likely to be passed between people / fewer carriers [B1]
Chains of transmission are broken [B1]
So unvaccinated people (e.g. babies, immunocompromised) are unlikely to meet an infected person [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the influenza vaccine must be changed each year, but the measles vaccine does not. (4)
hints: Do memory cells still recognise the pathogen?
questions.solution:
The influenza virus mutates frequently, changing its surface antigens [B1]
Memory cells / antibodies from earlier vaccines are not complementary to new antigens [B1]
Measles antigens change very little [B1]
So memory cells from vaccination still recognise measles [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which cells release antibodies into the blood?

Choose one answer.

A  Macrophages
B  T helper cells
C  Plasma cells
D  Memory B cells (1)
hints: They have lots of rough ER.
questions.solution: C — plasma cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the cells that release cytokines to activate B cells. (1)
questions.solution: T helper cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the cells that destroy body cells infected with a virus. (1)
questions.solution: T killer (cytotoxic) cells [B1]

questions.prompt:
What type of immunity is given by a vaccination?

Choose one answer.

A  Active artificial
B  Active natural
C  Passive artificial
D  Passive natural (1)
hints: Does the person make their own antibodies?
questions.solution: A — active artificial. [B1]

questions.prompt: A baby receives antibodies in its mother's milk. Name this type of immunity. (1)
hints: The baby doesn't make the antibodies.
questions.solution: Passive natural immunity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why passive immunity only lasts for a short time. (1)
questions.solution: Antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are made, as the immune system has not been activated [B1]

questions.prompt:
The measles virus destroys some memory B cells and antibodies made against other pathogens.

Explain why children may need to repeat other vaccinations after recovering from measles. (3)
hints: Without them, what happens on reinfection?
questions.solution:
Memory cells give a fast secondary response to a pathogen [B1]
If they are destroyed, there would only be a slow primary response [B1]
So the child could develop the disease before enough antibodies are made [B1]
Re-vaccination makes new memory cells [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the secondary immune response is faster and larger than the primary response. (3)
questions.solution:
Memory B and T cells remain after the primary response [B1]
They recognise the antigen quickly and divide rapidly by mitosis [B1]
Memory B cells differentiate into plasma cells, producing more antibodies faster [B1]
Pathogen destroyed before symptoms develop [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of B cells after a pathogen enters the body for the first time. (3)
hints: Two types of cell are produced.
questions.solution:
B cell with a complementary receptor binds the antigen [B1]
Activated by cytokines from T helper cells; divides by mitosis (clonal expansion) [B1]
Differentiates into plasma cells that secrete antibodies [B1]
And memory B cells [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Name the type of response in which phagocytes engulf bacteria shortly after they enter the body. (1)
hints: It does not depend on a particular antigen.
questions.solution: Non-specific response [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the protein released by virus-infected cells that stops viral replication in nearby cells. (1)
questions.solution: Interferon [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one way in which inflammation helps fight infection. (1)
questions.solution: Vasodilation / increased permeability lets more phagocytes and antibodies reach the infected tissue [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the bacteria that cause tuberculosis can stay dormant in the body without being destroyed by the immune system. (3)
questions.solution:
Bacteria are engulfed by macrophages but survive inside them [B1]
They have a thick waxy cell wall resistant to digestion / prevent lysosomes fusing with the phagosome [B1]
Infected macrophages are walled off in tubercles / granulomas [B1]
So antibodies / T cells can't reach them [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the symptoms of tuberculosis and explain how it is transmitted. (3)
questions.solution:
Persistent cough / coughing up blood, weight loss, fever, night sweats [B1]
Destruction of lung tissue [B1]
Transmitted by droplets coughed or sneezed by an infected person [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why tuberculosis is treated with several antibiotics for at least six months. (3)
questions.solution:
Bacteria are slow-growing / hidden inside macrophages and tubercles, so hard to reach [B1]
Long treatment needed to kill all bacteria [B1]
Several antibiotics reduce the chance of resistance developing [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
In one year, 1.4 million HIV-positive people had TB, and 520 000 of them died from TB.

Calculate the percentage of HIV-positive TB patients who died. (2)

8.0 million HIV-negative people had TB and 1.28 million died.

Calculate the percentage who died, and compare it with a death rate of 37 % for HIV-positive patients. (2)
questions.solution:
1.28 ÷ 8.0 × 100 = 16 % [M1]
HIV-positive patients more than twice as likely to die (37 vs 16 %) [A1]

questions.prompt:
Of 9.4 million TB cases, 15 % were in HIV-positive people.

Calculate the number of HIV-positive people with TB. (2)
questions.solution:
9.4 million × 0.15 [M1]
= 1.41 million [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with HIV are more likely to die from tuberculosis. (2)
hints: HIV destroys a type of immune cell.
questions.solution:
HIV destroys T helper cells, so fewer B cells and T killer cells are activated [B1]
So TB bacteria are not controlled / dormant TB becomes active [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why HIV infection leads to AIDS. (2)
hints: What happens to T helper cell numbers over time?
questions.solution:
HIV replicates in and destroys T helper cells [B1]
As numbers fall, the immune system can't respond, so opportunistic infections develop (AIDS) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how HIV replicates inside a T helper cell. (2)
hints: Viral DNA joins the host DNA.
questions.solution:
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from viral RNA; integrase inserts it into the host DNA [B1]
Host cell transcribes and translates viral genes to make new virus particles, which bud out [B1]

questions.prompt:
The incidence of TB is higher in people with lower T helper cell counts.

Explain how antiviral drugs for HIV could reduce the number of deaths from TB. (6)
hints: How do antivirals affect HIV and T helper cells?
Link T helper cells to control of TB.
questions.solution:
Antivirals (e.g. reverse transcriptase inhibitors) stop HIV replicating [B1]
Fewer T helper cells destroyed; T helper count rises [B1]
More cytokines released, activating B cells and T killer cells [B1]
More antibodies and better phagocyte activity against TB [B1]
So TB stays dormant / is destroyed; fewer active TB cases [B1]
Fewer TB deaths; also less transmission of TB to others [B1]
Level-marked: a logically linked explanation (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Discuss the difficulties of controlling tuberculosis worldwide. (6)
hints: Think about poverty, HIV and antibiotics.
questions.solution:
Spread by droplets in overcrowded / poorly ventilated housing [B1]
HIV makes people more vulnerable [B1]
Long courses of several antibiotics; patients may not finish them [B1]
Multidrug-resistant strains [B1]
BCG vaccine only partly effective, especially in adults [B1]
Cost / poor access to healthcare and diagnosis in poorer countries [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain the evolutionary race between pathogens and their hosts, using examples. (6)
hints: Each adaptation in the host selects for a counter-adaptation in the pathogen.
questions.solution:
Hosts evolve defences such as specific immunity [B1]
Pathogens evolve ways to evade them [B1]
e.g. TB survives inside macrophages and stops lysosomes fusing [B1]
e.g. HIV destroys T helper cells / mutates rapidly, changing antigens [B1]
Natural selection favours pathogens that evade defences and hosts with better defences [B1]
This cycle continues — neither 'wins' permanently [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the brain reduces heart rate after exercise. (2)
hints: Which part of the brain controls heart rate?
questions.solution:
Cardiovascular control centre in the medulla oblongata detects the fall in CO₂ / rise in pH (via chemoreceptors) [B1]
Sends more impulses along the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve to the SAN, slowing heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how heart rate increases at the start of exercise. (2)
hints: Which receptors detect CO₂ and muscle movement?
Which nerve speeds up the SAN?
questions.solution:
Chemoreceptors detect rise in CO₂ / fall in pH; stretch receptors detect muscle movement [B1]
Medulla sends more impulses along the sympathetic nerve to the SAN, increasing heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how adrenaline increases cardiac output during exercise. (2)
hints: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Adrenaline acts on the SAN and cardiac muscle.
questions.solution:
Adrenaline increases the rate of firing of the SAN, so heart rate increases [B1]
And increases the force of contraction, so stroke volume increases [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the brain reduces sweating after exercise. (2)
hints: Which part of the brain detects blood temperature?
questions.solution:
Hypothalamus / thermoregulatory centre detects the fall in core / blood temperature [B1]
Fewer impulses sent to sweat glands, so less sweat produced [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how vasodilation of skin arterioles helps cool the body during exercise. (2)
hints: How does heat leave the skin?
questions.solution:
Arterioles in the skin dilate, so more blood flows near the skin surface [B1]
More heat lost by radiation / conduction / convection [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sweating is less effective at cooling the body in humid conditions. (2)
hints: What does high humidity do to evaporation?
questions.solution:
Sweat cools the body when it evaporates, taking latent heat from the skin [B1]
In humid air, the water vapour gradient is smaller, so less sweat evaporates [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why too much exercise could be harmful to the body. (3)
hints: Think about joints and the immune system.
questions.solution:
Damage / wear to joints, e.g. cartilage, ligaments, tendons [B1]
Suppression of the immune system / fewer natural killer cells, so more infections [B1]
Dehydration / overheating [B1]
Muscle damage / stress fractures [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why moderate exercise reduces the risk of coronary heart disease. (3)
hints: Think about blood pressure and blood lipids.
questions.solution:
Lowers blood pressure, so less damage to the endothelium [B1]
Increases HDL / reduces LDL, so less atheroma formation [B1]
Helps reduce body mass / obesity [B1]
Reduces risk of type 2 diabetes / improves insulin sensitivity [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss whether athletes should be allowed to use performance-enhancing drugs such as anabolic steroids. (3)
hints: Think about health, fairness and choice.
questions.solution:
Against: unfair advantage over athletes who don't use them [B1]
Against: health risks, e.g. liver damage, heart disease, infertility [B1]
Against: athletes may feel pressured to use them [B1]
For: athletes are adults who can make informed choices / testing is expensive [B1]
Any 3, with both sides considered — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Where is the myosin-binding site found in a muscle fibre?

Choose one answer.

A  Actin
B  Sarcoplasmic reticulum
C  Tropomyosin
D  Troponin (1)
hints: Myosin heads bind to the thin filament.
Tropomyosin covers the site at rest.
questions.solution: A — actin. [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which ion binds to troponin to start muscle contraction?

Choose one answer.

A  Na⁺
B  K⁺
C  Ca²⁺
D  Cl⁻ (1)
hints: It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
questions.solution: C — Ca²⁺. [B1]

questions.prompt: Which band of a sarcomere stays the same length when a muscle contracts? (1)
hints: It is the length of the myosin filaments.
questions.solution: The A band [B1]

questions.prompt:
An actin filament is made of many globular actin monomers joined into a twisted chain. Collagen is made of three polypeptide chains wound around each other.

Compare and contrast the structures of actin filaments and collagen. (3)
hints: Both are proteins made of amino acids.
One is globular-based, the other fibrous.
questions.solution:
Similarity: both are made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds [B1]
Similarity: both are made of several polypeptides / have quaternary structure / are helical [B1]
Difference: actin is made of globular subunits; collagen is fibrous [B1]
Difference: collagen has three polypeptides held by hydrogen bonds; actin has many monomers [B1]
Any 3, including a similarity and a difference — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Compare the structure of haemoglobin with the structure of collagen. (3)
hints: Think about prosthetic groups and repeating sequences.
questions.solution:
Both have quaternary structure (haemoglobin 4 polypeptides; collagen 3) [B1]
Haemoglobin is globular and soluble; collagen is fibrous and insoluble [B1]
Haemoglobin contains a haem prosthetic group; collagen has none [B1]
Collagen has a repeating amino acid sequence (every third glycine); haemoglobin does not [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of collagen makes it suitable for its role in tendons. (3)
hints: Think about how the chains are held together.
questions.solution:
Three polypeptide chains wound into a triple helix [B1]
Held by many hydrogen bonds between chains [B1]
Covalent cross-links between molecules form fibrils and fibres [B1]
Gives high tensile strength / does not stretch [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how troponin and tropomyosin interact to allow muscle contraction. (2)
hints: What blocks the binding sites at rest?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions bind to troponin, changing its shape [B1]
Troponin pulls tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of ATP in the sliding filament mechanism. (2)
hints: ATP is needed for the head to detach.
questions.solution:
ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from actin [B1]
ATP is hydrolysed, causing the myosin head to return to its original position / re-cock [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why muscles relax when nervous stimulation stops. (2)
hints: What happens to the binding sites?
questions.solution:
Calcium ions are actively transported back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Tropomyosin covers the binding sites again, so no actin–myosin cross-bridges form [B1]

questions.prompt:
The myosin head contains an ATPase enzyme.

Explain the importance of primary structure for the function of this enzyme. (3)
hints: What must the active site fit?
questions.solution:
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids [B1]
Determines the folding / tertiary structure, via bonds between R groups [B1]
So determines the shape of the active site [B1]
Which must be complementary to ATP so it can be hydrolysed [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a mutation in the gene for a muscle enzyme might reduce the rate of contraction. (3)
questions.solution:
Changes the base sequence, so a different amino acid sequence [B1]
So the tertiary structure / active site shape changes [B1]
Substrate no longer fits / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
Less ATP hydrolysed, so fewer cross-bridge cycles [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Compare slow-twitch and fast-twitch muscle fibres. (3)
hints: Think about respiration type and fatigue.
questions.solution:
Slow-twitch have more mitochondria / mainly aerobic respiration [B1]
Slow-twitch have more myoglobin and capillaries (red) [B1]
Fast-twitch contract faster and more powerfully but fatigue quickly [B1]
Fast-twitch rely more on anaerobic respiration / have more glycogen and creatine phosphate [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Deduce what happens to lactate after it is absorbed from the blood by liver cells. (2)
hints: Lactate is converted back to something useful.
What does the liver need oxygen for?
questions.solution:
Lactate is oxidised / converted back to pyruvate (using oxygen — repaying the oxygen debt) [B1]
Pyruvate is used in aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle) or converted to glucose / glycogen [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why converting pyruvate to lactate allows glycolysis to continue during intense exercise. (2)
hints: What happens to reduced NAD when pyruvate becomes lactate?
questions.solution:
Reduced NAD is oxidised when pyruvate is reduced to lactate [B1]
So NAD is regenerated and can accept hydrogen in glycolysis again, allowing some ATP to be made [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why anaerobic respiration produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration. (2)
questions.solution:
Only glycolysis takes place / no link reaction, Krebs cycle or electron transport chain [B1]
Oxidative phosphorylation (the main source of ATP) needs oxygen as the final electron acceptor [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the liver is an organ rather than a tissue. (2)
hints: An organ contains several of them.
questions.solution:
A tissue is a group of similar cells with the same function [B1]
The liver contains several different tissues working together to carry out a function [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why xylem is described as a tissue. (2)
questions.solution:
It is made of several types of cell (vessels, fibres, parenchyma) [B1]
Working together to carry out one function — transporting water and providing support [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the heart is described as an organ. (2)
hints: Name some tissues in the heart.
questions.solution:
It contains different tissues, e.g. cardiac muscle, connective tissue, epithelium, nervous tissue [B1]
Working together to pump blood [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the stage of aerobic respiration that produces no ATP. (1)
hints: It happens between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
questions.solution: The link reaction [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. (1)
questions.solution: Oxygen [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the location of the Krebs cycle in a cell. (1)
questions.solution: Mitochondrial matrix [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why some ATP is used up at the start of glycolysis. (2)
questions.solution:
ATP is hydrolysed to phosphorylate glucose (to hexose bisphosphate) [B1]
Making it more reactive / lowering activation energy so it can be split into two triose phosphates [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the net yield of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule, and explain your answer. (2)
hints: How many ATP are used and how many made?
Two triose phosphates each give 2 ATP.
questions.solution:
2 ATP used, 4 ATP made [B1]
Net gain = 2 ATP per glucose [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why respiration of fatty acids releases more energy per gram than respiration of glucose. (2)
questions.solution:
Fatty acids contain more hydrogen atoms per gram [B1]
So more reduced NAD / FAD formed, giving more ATP in the electron transport chain [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of the carrier molecules in the electron transport chain. (3)
questions.solution:
Carriers accept and pass on electrons from reduced NAD / FAD (redox reactions) [B1]
Energy released is used to pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) [B1]
Producing ATP from ADP and Pi; oxygen is the final acceptor [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Cyanide inhibits the final carrier in the electron transport chain. Explain why cyanide is lethal. (3)
hints: What happens to the flow of electrons?
questions.solution:
Electrons cannot be passed to oxygen, so the chain stops [B1]
No proton gradient / no H⁺ pumped, so ATP synthase cannot make ATP [B1]
Reduced NAD not oxidised, so Krebs cycle and link reaction also stop [B1]
Cells don't get enough ATP for processes such as muscle contraction [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a mitochondrion is adapted for oxidative phosphorylation. (3)
hints: What does the intermembrane space allow?
questions.solution:
Inner membrane folded into cristae gives a large surface area [B1]
For many electron carriers and ATP synthase [B1]
Small intermembrane space allows a high concentration of H⁺ to build up [B1]
Inner membrane impermeable to H⁺ except through ATP synthase [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
In mice, the aorta became less elastic when they were given the anabolic steroid nandrolone. Exercise alone made the aorta more elastic.

Explain how nandrolone use could lead to atherosclerosis. (3)
hints: Less elastic arteries mean higher blood pressure.
How does high pressure start atherosclerosis?
questions.solution:
Less elastic aorta can't stretch and recoil, so blood pressure rises [B1]
High pressure damages the endothelium [B1]
Inflammatory response; LDL cholesterol and white blood cells build up under the endothelium [B1]
Forming an atheroma / plaque that narrows the artery [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how anabolic steroids increase muscle mass. (3)
questions.solution:
Steroids are lipid-soluble, so diffuse through the cell membrane [B1]
They bind to receptors in the cytoplasm, forming a hormone–receptor complex [B1]
The complex acts as a transcription factor, increasing transcription of genes for muscle proteins [B1]
More protein synthesis / muscle growth [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why some endurance athletes illegally use erythropoietin (EPO), and one risk of doing so. (3)
hints: EPO stimulates red blood cell production.
questions.solution:
EPO stimulates production of more red blood cells [B1]
So more oxygen carried to muscles / more aerobic respiration, delaying fatigue [B1]
Risk: blood becomes more viscous, increasing risk of clots / stroke / heart attack [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
In mice, exercise alone increased aorta elasticity, increased the activity of electron transport chain complexes, and increased Tfam mRNA (a factor that increases mitochondrial DNA). Mice given nandrolone with exercise showed smaller increases or decreases in all three.

Discuss the advantages of an exercise programme without nandrolone. (6)
hints: Link each result to a health benefit.
Mention the limitations of mouse studies.
questions.solution:
Exercise alone increased elasticity of the aorta, lowering blood pressure and risk of atherosclerosis [B1]
Nandrolone cancelled / reduced this benefit [B1]
Exercise increased ETC activity, so more ATP from aerobic respiration [B1]
Exercise increased Tfam, suggesting more mitochondria / greater aerobic capacity [B1]
Nandrolone reduced these improvements, reducing endurance [B1]
But results are from mice, may not apply to humans; SDs overlap for some data [B1]
Level-marked: a full answer uses all three sets of data with limitations (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Discuss the benefits and risks of regular endurance exercise on the human body. (6)
hints: Think about the heart, muscles, lungs and immune system.
questions.solution:
Increased stroke volume / cardiac output, lower resting heart rate [B1]
More mitochondria, capillaries and myoglobin in muscles; better aerobic capacity [B1]
Lower blood pressure and LDL, reduced CVD risk [B1]
Reduced risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes [B1]
Risks: joint wear, injury [B1]
Risks: immune suppression with excessive training; dehydration [B1]
Level-marked: a balanced discussion (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how aerobic training changes the body so that an athlete can exercise for longer before fatigue sets in. (6)
hints: Think about the heart and lungs.
Think about the muscle fibres themselves.
questions.solution:
Cardiac muscle enlarges, increasing stroke volume and cardiac output [B1]
Increased tidal volume / vital capacity of the lungs [B1]
More capillaries in muscles, so better oxygen supply [B1]
More mitochondria and myoglobin in slow-twitch fibres [B1]
More aerobic respiration, so less lactate produced / anaerobic threshold delayed [B1]
More glycogen and fat stores available for respiration [B1]
Level-marked: a logical explanation linking changes to delayed fatigue (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion. (2)
questions.solution:
Double membrane (envelope), with the inner membrane folded into cristae [B1]
Matrix containing enzymes, ribosomes and circular DNA [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a chloroplast. (2)
questions.solution:
Double membrane, with thylakoid membranes stacked into grana [B1]
Stroma containing enzymes, starch grains, ribosomes and circular DNA [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two features of mitochondria that suggest they were once free-living prokaryotes. (2)
hints: Think about their DNA and ribosomes.
questions.solution:
Contain circular DNA / 70S ribosomes like bacteria [B1]
Have a double membrane / divide by binary fission [B1]

questions.prompt:
On an ECG, the time between two consecutive R peaks is 0.48 s.

Calculate the heart rate and the percentage increase above 100 beats per minute. (2)
hints: Heart rate = 60 ÷ time for one beat.

questions.prompt:
An ECG shows 18 R waves in 12 seconds.

Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute. (2)
questions.solution:
18 ÷ 12 = 1.5 beats per second [M1]
1.5 × 60 = 90 beats per minute [A1]

questions.prompt:
A person's stroke volume is 70 cm³ and heart rate is 72 beats per minute.

Calculate the cardiac output in dm³ per minute. (2)
hints: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
questions.solution:
70 × 72 = 5040 cm³ per minute [M1]
= 5.04 dm³ per minute [A1]

questions.prompt: Which event does the QRS complex on an ECG show? (1)
questions.solution: Depolarisation of the ventricles (just before ventricular contraction) [B1]

questions.prompt: What does the P wave on an ECG show? (1)
questions.solution: Depolarisation of the atria [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why there is a short delay between the P wave and the QRS complex. (1)
questions.solution: The AV node delays the impulse so the atria finish contracting and ventricles fill before they contract [B1]

questions.prompt:
Acetylcholine released from the vagus nerve slows the heart. A poison blocks acetylcholine receptors on cells of the sinoatrial node.

Explain why the poison increases heart rate. (3)
hints: What normally happens when ACh binds to SAN cells?
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine can't bind to receptors on the SAN [B1]
So parasympathetic / vagus stimulation has no effect [B1]
SAN fires at its intrinsic rate / sympathetic effect dominates, so heart rate rises [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the sinoatrial node coordinates a heartbeat. (3)
questions.solution:
SAN generates a wave of depolarisation that spreads across the atria, which contract [B1]
A layer of non-conducting tissue prevents it reaching the ventricles directly; AV node delays it [B1]
Passes down the bundle of His and Purkyne fibres, so ventricles contract from the apex upwards [B1]

questions.prompt:
A drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase at synapses between the vagus nerve and the SAN.

Explain why this lowers heart rate. (3)
hints: What happens to ACh in the cleft?
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine is not broken down, so stays in the synaptic cleft [B1]
It continues to bind to receptors on SAN cells [B1]
Greater parasympathetic effect, so SAN fires less often and heart rate falls [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of vital capacity. (1)
questions.solution: The maximum volume of air that can be breathed out after a maximum breath in [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of tidal volume. (1)
questions.solution: The volume of air breathed in (or out) in one normal breath [B1]

questions.prompt: A spirometer trace shows a tidal volume of 0.5 dm³ and 15 breaths per minute. Calculate the minute ventilation. (1)
hints: Minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.

questions.prompt: Describe how acetylcholine crosses a neuromuscular junction. (2)
questions.solution:
Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release acetylcholine by exocytosis [B1]
Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the motor end plate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an impulse at a neuromuscular junction leads to muscle contraction. (2)
questions.solution:
Depolarisation spreads along the sarcolemma and down T-tubules [B1]
Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, triggering contraction [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between a neuromuscular junction and a synapse between two neurones. (2)
questions.solution:
NMJ is always excitatory; neurone synapses can be excitatory or inhibitory [B1]
NMJ links a neurone to a muscle (motor end plate, effector); one action potential always triggers a response [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why core body temperature rises during the first 20 minutes of exercise. (2)
hints: Where does the heat come from?
Why can't it all be lost at once?
questions.solution:
Increased respiration in muscles releases heat [B1]
Heat production is greater than heat loss until thermoregulation (sweating, vasodilation) catches up [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the body increases heat production when core temperature falls. (2)
questions.solution:
Shivering — rapid involuntary muscle contractions that increase respiration [B1]
Increased metabolic rate (e.g. thyroxine / adrenaline) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why thermoregulation is an example of negative feedback. (2)
hints: What does the response do to the change?
questions.solution:
A change from the set point is detected by the hypothalamus [B1]
Responses reverse the change and return temperature to the set point [B1]

questions.prompt:
Nine athletes ran for 50 minutes in warm, humid conditions and in cool, dry conditions. Core temperature rose more in the warm, humid conditions. A student concluded that thermoregulation only works in cool, dry conditions.

Comment on this conclusion. (4)
hints: Did temperature keep rising in the warm conditions?
questions.solution:
Thermoregulation also works in warm conditions — temperature levelled off / returned to normal afterwards [B1]
Cooling is less effective in humid air because less sweat evaporates [B1]
Small sample of nine athletes; may not apply to others [B1]
Two variables changed (temperature and humidity), so can't tell which caused the difference [B1]

questions.prompt: A study found that marathon runners who drank more water had a lower rise in core temperature. Comment on the conclusion that drinking water keeps runners cooler. (4)
questions.solution:
Plausible: more water means more sweat production and evaporation [B1]
Correlation only; other factors may differ (fitness, pace, body mass) [B1]
Sample size / conditions not stated [B1]
Need a controlled study varying only water intake [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation. (4)
questions.solution:
Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect blood temperature [B1]
It also receives impulses from thermoreceptors in the skin [B1]
Sends impulses via the autonomic nervous system to effectors [B1]
e.g. sweat glands, skin arterioles, erector muscles, skeletal muscles (shivering) [B1]

questions.prompt:
After exercise, core temperature fell from 39.2 °C to 37.4 °C in 30 minutes in cool conditions, but only from 39.8 °C to 38.6 °C in warm, humid conditions.

Compare and contrast the changes. (3)
questions.solution:
Similarity: temperature decreased in both [B1]
Difference: fall was larger in cool conditions (1.8 °C vs 1.2 °C) [B1]
Difference: temperature stayed higher / did not return to normal in warm conditions [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the mean rate of fall in core temperature in each condition from the previous data (cool: 39.2 → 37.4 °C; warm: 39.8 → 38.6 °C, both in 30 minutes). (3)
questions.solution:
Cool: 1.8 ÷ 30 = 0.06 °C min⁻¹ [M1]
Warm: 1.2 ÷ 30 = 0.04 °C min⁻¹ [M1]
Cooling 1.5 times faster in cool conditions [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why core temperature falls faster after exercise in cool, dry conditions than in warm, humid conditions. (3)
questions.solution:
Larger temperature gradient between the skin and air, so more heat lost by radiation / convection [B1]
Dry air means more sweat evaporates, removing more heat [B1]
In humid air sweat drips off without evaporating, so less cooling [B1]

questions.prompt:
Neutrophil concentration fell from 3.57 × 10⁶ to 3.42 × 10⁶ cells cm⁻³ after exercise. A person has 5 dm³ of blood and a mass of 70 kg.

Calculate how many fewer neutrophils there are per kg of body mass. (3)
questions.solution:
Difference = 0.15 × 10⁶ cells cm⁻³ [M1]
× 5000 cm³ = 7.5 × 10⁸ cells [M1]
÷ 70 kg = 1.07 × 10⁷ cells kg⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt:
Natural killer cell counts fell from 0.30 × 10⁶ to 0.18 × 10⁶ cells cm⁻³ after a marathon.

Calculate the percentage decrease and suggest one consequence. (3)
questions.solution:
(0.30 − 0.18) ÷ 0.30 × 100 [M1]
= 40 % [A1]
Greater risk of infection, e.g. upper respiratory tract infections [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why moderate exercise improves immunity but very intense exercise may reduce it. (3)
questions.solution:
Moderate exercise increases numbers / activity of natural killer cells and phagocytes [B1]
Intense exercise reduces NK cells, phagocyte activity and antibody (IgA) levels [B1]
Possibly due to stress hormones such as cortisol [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a fall in neutrophil numbers after exercise could increase the risk of infection. (1)
questions.solution: Fewer phagocytes to engulf and destroy pathogens [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the process by which neutrophils engulf bacteria. (1)
questions.solution: Phagocytosis [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the organelle in neutrophils that contains enzymes to digest engulfed bacteria. (1)
questions.solution: Lysosome [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain one way in which cartilage at the ends of bones in a knee joint reduces wear. (2)
questions.solution:
Cartilage is smooth, so reduces friction between bones as they move [B1]
Absorbs shock / compression, so bones don't rub or crack [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of ligaments and tendons in movement at a joint. (2)
questions.solution:
Ligaments join bone to bone, holding the joint together / limiting movement [B1]
Tendons join muscle to bone, transmitting the force of contraction [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antagonistic muscles cause movement at the elbow. (2)
questions.solution:
Muscles can only pull, so work in pairs [B1]
Biceps contracts (triceps relaxes) to flex the arm; triceps contracts (biceps relaxes) to extend it [B1]

questions.prompt: State which type of brain scan uses X-rays, and which uses magnetic fields and radio waves. (2)
questions.solution:
X-rays: CT (computerised tomography) [B1]
Magnetic fields and radio waves: MRI [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how fMRI shows which areas of the brain are active during a task. (2)
hints: Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin respond differently to the magnetic field.
questions.solution:
Active areas of the brain receive more blood / oxygenated blood [B1]
fMRI detects the difference between oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin, so active areas show up [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage of an MRI scan over a CT scan for investigating a brain tumour, and one disadvantage. (2)
hints: Think about detail of soft tissue and radiation.
Think about time, cost and metal implants.
questions.solution:
Advantage: better image of soft tissue / no ionising radiation [B1]
Disadvantage: takes longer / more expensive / can't be used with metal implants / noisy [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a PET scan can be used to investigate the brain. (2)
hints: Which areas take up the most tracer?
questions.solution:
A radioactive tracer (e.g. labelled glucose) is injected [B1]
More active areas take up more tracer, which is detected to show activity / location of tumours [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a PET scan could show reduced dopamine activity in the brain of a person with Parkinson's disease. (2)
hints: Tracers can be attached to molecules that bind to dopamine receptors or transporters.
questions.solution:
A radioactive tracer that binds dopamine transporters / receptors (or labelled L-dopa) is used [B1]
Less tracer detected in the striatum / dopamine areas compared with a healthy brain [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why PET scans are not used routinely for healthy people. (2)
questions.solution:
Uses ionising radiation / radioactive tracer, which carries a risk [B1]
Expensive / limited availability / tracers have short half-lives [B1]

questions.prompt:
A child is shown a cheeseburger every 5 minutes. The mass of saliva produced was 2.0 g after the first viewing and fell steadily to 0.4 g by the eighth viewing.

Describe the effect on saliva production and name this type of learning. (2)
hints: The response decreases to a repeated harmless stimulus.
questions.solution:
Saliva production decreases with repeated exposure, from 2.0 g to 0.4 g (80 % decrease) [B1]
Habituation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why habituation is an advantage to animals. (2)
hints: What would happen if they responded to every harmless stimulus?
questions.solution:
Animals stop responding to repeated, harmless stimuli [B1]
So they save energy / time for important stimuli such as predators or food [B1]

questions.prompt:
A sea slug withdraws its gill when touched. After repeated gentle touches it stops withdrawing it, but a different stimulus produces the full response again.

Explain why this shows habituation rather than muscle fatigue. (2)
hints: What is specific to the repeated stimulus?
questions.solution:
The response returns with a new stimulus, so the muscle can still contract (not fatigued) [B1]
The decrease is specific to the repeated harmless stimulus / due to changes at synapses [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what happens at synapses that causes a response to decrease after repeated stimulation (habituation). (4)
hints: Think about calcium channels in the presynaptic knob.
questions.solution:
Fewer calcium ion channels open in the presynaptic membrane / less Ca²⁺ enters [B1]
So fewer vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane [B1]
Less neurotransmitter is released into the cleft [B1]
Fewer neurotransmitter molecules bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Fewer Na⁺ channels open / threshold not reached, so no action potential in the postsynaptic neurone [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how an impulse is passed across a cholinergic synapse. (4)
hints: Start with the action potential arriving.
End with the neurotransmitter being removed.
questions.solution:
Action potential arrives; Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ diffuses into the presynaptic knob [B1]
Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine by exocytosis [B1]
Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters, depolarisation; action potential if threshold reached [B1]
Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how MDMA (ecstasy) affects synapses in the brain that use serotonin. (4)
hints: What happens to the concentration in the cleft?
questions.solution:
MDMA blocks / reverses serotonin reuptake transporters [B1]
So serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft [B1]
More serotonin binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
More action potentials / prolonged stimulation, giving the drug's mood effects [B1]
Can lead to depletion of serotonin afterwards [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of sodium ions in the functioning of a rod cell. (3)
hints: In the dark, Na⁺ flows in.
What happens when light breaks down rhodopsin?
questions.solution:
In the dark, Na⁺ channels are open and Na⁺ diffuses in, so the rod cell is depolarised [B1]
It releases neurotransmitter (glutamate) that inhibits the bipolar cell [B1]
In light, rhodopsin breaks down and Na⁺ channels close; Na⁺ is still pumped out [B1]
Rod is hyperpolarised, stops releasing neurotransmitter, so bipolar cell is depolarised [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why rod cells allow vision in dim light but give a low-resolution image. (3)
hints: Think about how many rods connect to one bipolar cell.
questions.solution:
Several rods synapse with one bipolar cell (retinal convergence) [B1]
Small amounts of neurotransmitter from many rods summate to reach threshold, so sensitive in dim light [B1]
But the brain can't tell which rod was stimulated, so low resolution / poor detail [B1]
Rhodopsin is very sensitive / bleached by low light [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a resting potential is maintained across the membrane of a neurone. (3)
hints: Which pump moves Na⁺ and K⁺?
questions.solution:
Sodium–potassium pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in [B1]
Membrane is more permeable to K⁺, so K⁺ diffuses back out [B1]
Membrane less permeable to Na⁺ / Na⁺ channels closed [B1]
So inside is negative relative to outside (about −70 mV) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Name the part of the brain that coordinates fine movements such as drawing a straight line. (1)
hints: It is at the back, under the cerebrum.
questions.solution: Cerebellum [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the brain that sends impulses to the sinoatrial node when the pH of the blood falls. (1)
questions.solution: Medulla oblongata [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the brain where synapses form during the critical period for vision. (1)
hints: At the back of the cerebrum.
questions.solution: Visual cortex (occipital lobe of the cerebral hemispheres) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a region of the brain appears brighter on an fMRI scan while a person carries out a task. (3)
questions.solution:
Neurones in that region are more active, so respire more and need more oxygen [B1]
More blood flow to that region / more oxygenated haemoglobin [B1]
fMRI detects the difference in magnetic properties of oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how fMRI could be used to find which area of the brain is used for recognising faces. (3)
questions.solution:
Scan the brain while the person looks at faces and while they look at other objects [B1]
Identify areas with more blood flow / activity only when viewing faces [B1]
Repeat with many people to see if the same area is used [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a CT scan produces an image of the brain. (3)
questions.solution:
X-rays are passed through the head from many angles [B1]
Denser tissues absorb more X-rays [B1]
A computer combines the images into cross-sectional slices [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a combined PET and CT scan may be better for diagnosing a cancer than either scan alone. (3)
hints: One shows structure, the other shows activity.
What do cancer cells do more of?
questions.solution:
CT shows structures / the location and size of a tumour [B1]
PET shows metabolic activity — cancer cells respire more, so take up more tracer [B1]
Combined scan shows exactly where active tumour tissue is, distinguishing it from inactive / scar tissue [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the use of MRI and fMRI in investigating the brain. (3)
questions.solution:
Both use magnetic fields and radio waves / no ionising radiation [B1]
MRI shows structure, e.g. tumours or damage [B1]
fMRI shows function / activity by detecting oxygenated blood flow in real time [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three advantages of using brain scans rather than post-mortem examination to study brain disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Can study a living patient / diagnose and treat the disease [B1]
Can follow changes over time / repeat scans [B1]
Can study brain activity during tasks (function, not just structure) [B1]
Non-invasive [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how the muscles of the iris interact to dilate the pupil in dim light. (3)
hints: There are radial and circular muscles.
questions.solution:
Radial muscles contract (sympathetic stimulation) [B1]
Circular muscles relax [B1]
So the pupil widens, letting more light in [B1]
Muscles are antagonistic [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe the reflex arc that causes the pupil to constrict in bright light. (3)
questions.solution:
Light detected by photoreceptors in the retina; impulses along the optic (sensory) nerve [B1]
To the midbrain / brain, which sends impulses along parasympathetic motor neurones [B1]
Circular muscles of the iris contract and radial muscles relax, so pupil constricts [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. (3)
questions.solution:
Both are parts of the autonomic nervous system, controlling involuntary actions [B1]
Sympathetic prepares the body for action — e.g. increases heart rate, dilates pupils [B1]
Parasympathetic has calming / resting effects — e.g. slows heart rate, constricts pupils; often uses acetylcholine [B1]

questions.prompt:
What is a typical threshold potential for a neurone?

Choose one answer.

A  −80 mV
B  −70 mV
C  −55 mV
D  +40 mV (1)
Explain what is meant by the all-or-nothing principle for action potentials. (1)
questions.solution: If the threshold is reached, an action potential of the same size always occurs; if not, none occurs [B1]

questions.prompt: How does the nervous system detect the strength of a stimulus, given that all action potentials are the same size? (1)
hints: Not size — what else can vary?
questions.solution: A stronger stimulus produces a higher frequency of action potentials [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the changes in sodium and potassium ion movements during an action potential, from depolarisation to repolarisation. (4)
questions.solution:
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ diffuses into the neurone [B1]
Inside becomes positive / depolarised (to about +40 mV) [B1]
Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open [B1]
K⁺ diffuses out, so the inside becomes negative again (repolarisation) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why impulses travel faster along myelinated neurones than unmyelinated neurones. (4)
questions.solution:
Myelin sheath (Schwann cells) insulates the axon [B1]
Depolarisation can only occur at nodes of Ranvier [B1]
Local currents jump from node to node (saltatory conduction) [B1]
So fewer depolarisations along the length / faster transmission [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an action potential is propagated along an unmyelinated axon. (4)
questions.solution:
Na⁺ entering at the depolarised region diffuses along the axon (local currents) [B1]
Depolarises the next region to threshold, opening voltage-gated Na⁺ channels [B1]
So a new action potential forms further along [B1]
The region behind is in its refractory period, so the impulse travels one way only [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a neurone becomes hyperpolarised after an action potential. (3)
questions.solution:
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are slow to close [B1]
So more K⁺ diffuses out than needed to restore resting potential [B1]
Inside becomes more negative than −70 mV; Na⁺/K⁺ pump then restores the resting potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of the refractory period. (3)
hints: Can another action potential happen straight away?
questions.solution:
During the refractory period Na⁺ channels can't open / another action potential can't be generated [B1]
So impulses travel in one direction only [B1]
And action potentials are separate, limiting the frequency of impulses [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an inhibitory neurotransmitter such as GABA makes it less likely that an action potential will occur in the postsynaptic neurone. (3)
hints: What happens to the membrane potential?
questions.solution:
GABA binds to receptors and opens Cl⁻ (or K⁺) channels [B1]
Cl⁻ diffuses in / K⁺ diffuses out, so the membrane is hyperpolarised [B1]
More Na⁺ must enter to reach threshold, so action potential less likely [B1]

questions.prompt: Devise a procedure to investigate the effect of cooking on the vitamin C content of cauliflower. (4)
hints: Which reagent is decolourised by vitamin C?
How will you turn titration volumes into a concentration?
questions.solution:
Use the same mass of raw and cooked cauliflower to make extracts with the same volume of water [B1]
Titrate each extract into a fixed volume and concentration of DCPIP [B1]
Record the volume needed to decolourise the DCPIP (end point) [B1]
Use a vitamin C solution of known concentration to calibrate / calculate concentration [B1]
Repeat and calculate a mean [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Devise a procedure to compare the vitamin C content of fresh orange juice and orange juice that has been stored in the fridge for 5 days. (4)
hints: DCPIP turns colourless when vitamin C is added.
Less juice needed = more vitamin C.
questions.solution:
Add a fixed volume of 1 % DCPIP to a test tube [B1]
Add juice drop by drop from a burette / pipette until the blue colour disappears; record the volume [B1]
Calibrate using a vitamin C solution of known concentration [B1]
Keep the temperature / DCPIP concentration / shaking the same for each juice [B1]
Repeat for each juice and calculate means; smaller volume = more vitamin C [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how you could produce a calibration curve to find the vitamin C concentration of an unknown fruit juice using DCPIP. (4)
hints: You need several solutions you know the concentration of.
Plot one variable against the other, then read off the unknown.
questions.solution:
Make a range of vitamin C solutions of known concentration (serial dilution) [B1]
Find the volume of each needed to decolourise a fixed volume of DCPIP [B1]
Plot volume needed against concentration [B1]
Find the volume of juice needed to decolourise the same volume of DCPIP [B1]
Read its concentration from the curve [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
Scientists want to study the order in which insect species colonise dead pigs, to help estimate time of death in humans.

Describe how this study could be carried out. (3)
hints: How do you make the pigs comparable?
What do you record, and how often?
questions.solution:
Use pigs of the same mass / breed / age / sex [B1]
Control or record a named abiotic factor (e.g. temperature, shade) [B1]
Identify and record which insect species (and life stages) are present [B1]
Sample at regular time intervals [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a forensic entomologist could use blowfly larvae found on a body to estimate time of death. (3)
hints: Blowflies lay eggs soon after death.
Larvae grow at a rate that depends on temperature.
questions.solution:
Blowflies lay eggs on a body within hours of death [B1]
Identify the stage / measure the length of the oldest larvae [B1]
Use known development rates at the recorded temperature to work out their age [B1]
Time of death is at least the age of the oldest larvae [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how knowledge of the succession of insect species on a body helps to estimate time of death. (3)
hints: Different species arrive at different times.
questions.solution:
Different insect species arrive in a predictable sequence [B1]
Each species colonises when conditions suit it, changing the body for the next [B1]
Identify the species present on the body [B1]
Compare with known succession data (for similar conditions) to estimate time since death [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Extracts of bean and pea seeds contain peptides that may kill bacteria.

Devise a procedure to compare the effect of each extract, and of the two extracts combined, on the growth of a bacterium. (4)
hints: Use agar plates and something to hold the extract.
How will you measure the effect?
questions.solution:
Spread the bacterium evenly on agar plates (aseptic technique) [B1]
Add discs soaked in / wells filled with each extract, and the combined extract [B1]
Include a control disc with water / solvent only [B1]
Incubate at a suitable temperature (e.g. 25 °C) for a set time (24–48 h) [B1]
Measure the diameter / area of each clear zone (zone of inhibition) and compare [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Devise a procedure to find out whether garlic extract or mint extract is more effective at inhibiting the growth of bacteria. (4)
hints: What variables must be kept the same for each disc?
Think about safety and aseptic technique.
questions.solution:
Use the same bacterium spread on agar plates using aseptic technique [B1]
Soak paper discs of the same size in the same concentration / volume of each extract [B1]
Use a control disc soaked in water / solvent [B1]
Incubate all plates at the same temperature and time; tape lids, don't seal fully [B1]
Measure the area of the clear zone; repeat and calculate means [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
A student measured the diameter of the clear zone around a disc of antibiotic as 18 mm. The disc itself had a diameter of 6 mm.

Calculate the area of the clear zone (not including the disc) and explain why area is a better measure than diameter. (4)
hints: Subtract the area of the disc.
questions.solution:
Area of whole circle = π × 9² = 254.5 mm² [M1]
Area of disc = π × 3² = 28.3 mm² [M1]
Clear zone = 254.5 − 28.3 = 226 mm² [A1]
Area is proportional to the amount of bacterial growth inhibited / diameter underestimates the difference between zones [B1]

questions.prompt:
Data on venous thrombosis (VTE) in two age groups:

Under 20 years: 1.3 % of people develop VTE; 49 % of these patients carry the factor V mutation.
Over 70 years: 34 % of people develop VTE; 21 % of these patients carry the factor V mutation.

Use the data to deduce the relative importance of genotype and environment in causing VTE. (4)
hints: In which age group is the mutation a bigger share of cases?
What explains most cases in older people?
questions.solution:
VTE is much more common in people over 70 [B1]
A higher proportion of young patients have the mutation [B1]
So genotype has a bigger influence in younger people [B1]
In older people, most cases occur without the mutation, so environmental / lifestyle factors (e.g. inactivity, surgery) are more important [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a study of identical (monozygotic) twins, if one twin had type 2 diabetes the other had it in 76 % of cases. For non-identical twins the figure was 40 %.

Explain what these data suggest about the causes of type 2 diabetes. (4)
hints: Identical twins share all their alleles; non-identical share about half.
questions.solution:
Identical twins are genetically identical; non-identical share about 50 % of alleles [B1]
The higher concordance in identical twins suggests a genetic component [B1]
Concordance is not 100 %, so environment / lifestyle also contributes [B1]
Twins often share an environment, so the genetic effect may be overestimated [B1]

questions.prompt:
A study found that people who ate the most salt had twice the rate of stroke of those who ate the least.

Discuss whether this shows that a high salt intake causes strokes. (4)
hints: What other factors might differ between the groups?
questions.solution:
There is a positive correlation between salt intake and stroke [B1]
But correlation does not prove causation [B1]
Other variables may be involved, e.g. smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, age [B1]
A plausible mechanism exists: salt raises blood pressure, which damages arteries [B1]
Need a controlled study / large sample / matched groups to confirm [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
The mean lifespan of fruit flies kept at different temperatures was:

15 °C: 130 days
21 °C: 86 days
27 °C: 42 days
30 °C: 20 days

Describe the relationship between temperature and lifespan. (2)
hints: Is the trend positive or negative?
questions.solution:
As temperature increases, lifespan decreases (negative correlation) [B1]
Quantified, e.g. lifespan falls by 110 days / about 85 % between 15 °C and 30 °C (about 7 days per °C) [B1]

questions.prompt:
The rate of heartbeat of a water flea was measured at different caffeine concentrations: 0 mM, 180 beats per min; 1 mM, 216; 2 mM, 252; 4 mM, 324.

Describe the relationship and calculate the percentage increase from 0 mM to 4 mM. (2)
questions.solution:
Heart rate increases as caffeine concentration increases (positive, roughly linear — 36 beats per mM) [B1]
(324 − 180) ÷ 180 × 100 = 80 % increase [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a positive correlation and a causal relationship. (2)
hints: One describes a pattern, the other an explanation.
What kind of evidence is needed for a causal link?
questions.solution:
A positive correlation means both variables increase together [B1]
A causal relationship means a change in one variable directly causes the change in the other — shown by a controlled experiment / known mechanism [B1]

questions.prompt:
A student thinks that the percentage of cells undergoing mitosis decreases with distance from a root tip.

Write a suitable null hypothesis. (1)
hints: A null hypothesis predicts no effect.
questions.solution: There is no correlation / relationship between distance from the root tip and the percentage of cells in mitosis [B1]

questions.prompt: Write a null hypothesis for an investigation into whether the mean number of stomata per mm² differs between the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf. (1)
questions.solution: There is no difference in the mean number of stomata per mm² between the upper and lower leaf surfaces [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a statistical test that could be used to find whether there is a correlation between distance from the root tip and the percentage of cells in mitosis. (1)
hints: You are looking for a correlation, not a difference.
The data may not be normally distributed.
questions.solution: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a student could use a microscope to compare the sizes of cells in two different regions of a root. (3)
hints: You need to calibrate an eyepiece graticule.
questions.solution:
Calibrate the eyepiece graticule against a stage micrometer [B1]
Measure the diameter / length of cells in each region in eyepiece units and convert to µm [B1]
Measure many cells (e.g. 20) chosen at random in each region [B1]
Calculate a mean for each region and compare (e.g. with a t-test) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
At ×400, 1 eyepiece unit = 2.5 µm. A cell measures 16 eyepiece units long.

Calculate the actual length of the cell, and explain why the graticule must be recalibrated if the objective lens is changed. (3)
questions.solution:
16 × 2.5 = 40 µm [M1 A1]
The eyepiece graticule stays the same size but the image is magnified differently, so each eyepiece unit represents a different length [B1]

questions.prompt:
A stage micrometer scale has divisions 10 µm apart. With a ×40 objective, 4 divisions of the stage micrometer line up with 25 eyepiece divisions.

Calculate the length represented by one eyepiece division. (3)
hints: Find the length of 4 stage micrometer divisions.
Divide by the number of eyepiece divisions.
questions.solution:
4 × 10 = 40 µm [M1]
40 ÷ 25 [M1]
= 1.6 µm per eyepiece division [A1]

questions.prompt:
In three countries, the percentage of men with prostate cancer rises from below 1 % at age 40 to around 10 % at age 80 in all three, though one country is always slightly higher.

Comment on the effect of age on the risk of developing prostate cancer. (3)
hints: Suggest why risk increases with age.
questions.solution:
Risk increases with age in all three countries [B1]
Use of figures, e.g. from about 1 % at 40 to about 10 % at 80 [B1]
More time for mutations to accumulate / longer exposure to carcinogens [B1]
Differences between countries suggest other factors (diet, screening, genetics) are involved [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the risk of developing cancer increases with age. (3)
hints: Cancer is caused by mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle.
questions.solution:
Cancer results from mutations in proto-oncogenes / tumour suppressor genes [B1]
Mutations accumulate over time / more cell divisions [B1]
More years of exposure to carcinogens / mutagens [B1]
DNA repair and immune surveillance become less effective with age [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Suggest three reasons why the recorded rate of a cancer might differ between countries. (3)
hints: Differences in genes, lifestyle and recording.
questions.solution:
Genetic differences between populations [B1]
Differences in diet / lifestyle / environment [B1]
Differences in screening or diagnosis rates [B1]
Differences in age structure / life expectancy of the population [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
A country has 2.86 million men. At a particular diet, the death rate from a cancer is 12.0 per 100 000 men.

Calculate the number of men expected to die from this cancer. (2)
hints: Find how many lots of 100 000 there are.

questions.prompt:
In a town of 64 000 people, 48 people developed a disease in one year.

Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people. (2)
hints: Divide the cases by the population.

questions.prompt:
The death rate from a disease fell from 160 to 112 per 100 000 people over ten years.

Calculate the percentage decrease. (2)
Explain why both identical and non-identical twins are included in studies of the causes of a disease. (2)
hints: Identical twins share all their alleles.
Both types usually share their environment.
questions.solution:
Identical twins have the same genotype; non-identical twins share about half their alleles [B1]
Both types share a similar environment, so comparing them shows whether genes or environment have the bigger effect [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why studying identical twins who were raised apart is particularly useful. (2)
hints: What is the same and what is different?
Which effect can then be isolated?
questions.solution:
They have identical genotypes but different environments [B1]
So any differences in phenotype must be due to environmental factors [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two limitations of using twin studies to work out the genetic contribution to a disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Sample sizes are often small [B1]
Twins' environments are not identical / identical twins may be treated more similarly than non-identical twins [B1]

questions.prompt:
Three studies investigated prostate cancer:
1. Rates rose with age in three countries.
2. Death rates were higher in countries with higher sugar intake.
3. If one identical twin developed prostate cancer, the other did in about 40 % of cases; for non-identical twins it was about 15 %.

Evaluate what these studies suggest about the causes of prostate cancer. (6)
hints: Comment on correlation, causation and limitations.
questions.solution:
Risk increases with age, suggesting accumulation of mutations [B1]
Positive correlation between sugar intake and death rate suggests diet / environment is a factor [B1]
But correlation does not prove causation; other factors may vary between countries [B1]
Higher concordance in identical twins suggests a genetic component [B1]
Concordance well below 100 % shows environment also matters [B1]
Conclusion: multifactorial — age, genes and lifestyle all contribute; limitations e.g. sample size, data from few countries [B1]
Level-marked: a full evaluation uses all three studies with a supported conclusion (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Studies of type 2 diabetes show: (1) people with a BMI over 30 are seven times more likely to develop it; (2) incidence has risen sharply in 30 years in countries where diets changed; (3) some ethnic groups have higher rates even at the same BMI.

Evaluate the relative importance of genetic and environmental factors in causing type 2 diabetes. (6)
hints: Which study points to environment and which to genes?
Could the rapid rise be genetic?
questions.solution:
Strong association between obesity and diabetes suggests lifestyle is important [B1]
Rapid rise over 30 years is too fast for genetic change, so environment / diet is the main cause [B1]
Higher rates in some ethnic groups at the same BMI suggest genetic susceptibility [B1]
Correlation does not prove causation / confounding factors [B1]
Genes and environment interact — a susceptible genotype is expressed in an obesogenic environment [B1]
Conclusion: both contribute; environment explains recent increases [B1]
Level-marked: a balanced evaluation with a supported conclusion (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
A newspaper reports that "drinking red wine prevents heart disease", based on a study of 500 people in one French town, where wine drinkers had 30 % less heart disease.

Evaluate this claim. (6)
hints: Think about sample size, representativeness and confounding variables.
questions.solution:
Only one study, with a small sample from one town — may not be representative [B1]
Correlation only; does not prove causation [B1]
Confounding variables, e.g. wine drinkers may be wealthier, eat more healthily, exercise more [B1]
Alcohol has known harmful effects (liver damage, high blood pressure) [B1]
Need peer review / repeated studies / controlled trials [B1]
Plausible mechanism (antioxidants / raised HDL) but claim "prevents" is too strong [B1]
Level-marked: a balanced evaluation with a supported conclusion (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Tfam mRNA (arbitrary units) in four groups of mice:
Control 100 ± 20
Nandrolone 75 ± 10
Exercise 170 ± 25
Exercise + nandrolone 85 ± 15
(± = standard deviation)

Explain why the conclusion that nandrolone reduces Tfam mRNA is not valid for all mice. (2)
hints: Look at whether the ranges overlap.
questions.solution:
Control (80–120) and nandrolone (65–85) ranges overlap [B1]
So the difference may not be significant / some nandrolone mice had higher values than some controls [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what a large standard deviation shows about a set of data. (2)
questions.solution:
The data are widely spread around the mean [B1]
So there is more variation / the mean is less reliable [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a statistical test that could show whether the difference between two group means is significant, and state when it is appropriate. (2)
hints: The data should be normally distributed.
questions.solution:
Student's t-test [B1]
For two sets of continuous data that are normally distributed / similar variances [B1]

questions.prompt:
Trees were removed and water levels raised to restore a peat bog.

Devise a procedure to measure how quickly the bog recovers. (4)
hints: What would you measure, and how often?
questions.solution:
Use quadrats placed randomly (random coordinates) across the bog [B1]
Measure percentage cover of sphagnum moss / species richness [B1]
Measure an abiotic factor, e.g. water table depth or pH [B1]
Repeat at regular intervals (e.g. every year) over several years [B1]
Compare with an undisturbed reference bog [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate how the distribution of plants changes from a footpath into an area of grassland. (4)
questions.solution:
Lay a tape measure (line transect) at right angles to the path [B1]
Place quadrats at regular intervals along the tape (belt / interrupted transect) [B1]
Record species present / percentage cover in each quadrat [B1]
Measure an abiotic factor at each point, e.g. soil compaction, light [B1]
Repeat transects at several places along the path [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would estimate the percentage cover of a plant species in a field, and why random sampling is important. (4)
hints: Use a grid and random numbers.
questions.solution:
Divide the field into a grid and generate random coordinates [B1]
Place quadrats at the coordinates [B1]
Estimate percentage cover by counting squares (or points) occupied [B1]
Use many quadrats and calculate a mean [B1]
Random sampling avoids bias [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt:
The observed numbers of alleles of one gene in a deer population were 4 (observed) compared with 6 (expected), and for another gene 3 (observed) compared with 5 (expected).

Calculate the χ² value for these two genes. Use χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E. (3)
hints: Calculate (O − E)² ÷ E for each gene.

questions.prompt:
A dihybrid cross gave 88 purple-smooth, 32 purple-wrinkled, 28 white-smooth and 12 white-wrinkled seeds (160 total). The expected ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Calculate the expected numbers and the χ² value. (3)

A χ² test on 4 categories gave a value of 9.2. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 3 degrees of freedom is 7.82.

Explain what this result shows. (3)
hints: Compare the calculated value with the critical value.
What happens to the null hypothesis?
questions.solution:
9.2 is greater than the critical value of 7.82 [B1]
So reject the null hypothesis [B1]
There is a significant difference between observed and expected results; probability of it being due to chance is less than 5 % [B1]

questions.prompt: Devise an investigation to compare the rate of the light-dependent reactions in chloroplasts from shade-tolerant and shade-intolerant plants. (6)
hints: What makes it a fair test?
questions.solution:
Grind leaves in cold, isotonic buffer; filter and centrifuge to isolate chloroplasts [B1]
Add chloroplast suspension to DCPIP (blue electron acceptor) [B1]
Expose to a fixed light intensity at a set distance; DCPIP decolourises as it is reduced [B1]
Measure the time / use a colorimeter to measure absorbance change [B1]
Control: same mass of leaf, volume of DCPIP, temperature; control tube in dark / without chloroplasts [B1]
Repeat for each species and compare mean rates [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Devise an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of an aquatic plant. (6)
questions.solution:
Place pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (CO₂ source) [B1]
Vary light intensity by changing the distance of a lamp (intensity ∝ 1/d²) [B1]
Measure volume of oxygen produced in a set time (photosynthometer / count bubbles) [B1]
Allow acclimatisation time at each distance [B1]
Control temperature (heat shield / water bath) and CO₂ concentration [B1]
Repeat at each intensity and calculate mean rates [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Devise an investigation to compare the photosynthetic pigments in shade-grown and sun-grown leaves of the same species. (6)
questions.solution:
Grind leaves with a solvent (e.g. propanone) to extract pigments [B1]
Spot extract repeatedly onto a pencil origin line on chromatography paper / TLC plate [B1]
Place in a running solvent below the origin line; lid on [B1]
Remove before the solvent reaches the top; mark the solvent front [B1]
Calculate Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent; identify pigments [B1]
Use same mass of leaf; compare number / intensity of spots between sun and shade leaves [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Scientists used mice of a single breed in an investigation into the effect of blood HDL levels on fertility.

Explain why this improves the investigation. (1)
hints: Valid = measures what it intends to.
questions.solution: Reduces genetic variation, which could affect fertility, so improves validity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision of results. (1)
questions.solution: Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value; precision is how close repeated results are to each other [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why investigations on animals use groups of several animals rather than single animals. (1)
