questions.solution: Individuals vary, so using several and calculating a mean reduces the effect of anomalies / allows statistical testing [B1]

questions.prompt: Write a null hypothesis for an investigation into the effect of blood plasma HDL concentration on the number of offspring produced by female mice. (1)
questions.solution: There is no correlation / no difference in the number of offspring produced at different HDL concentrations [B1]

questions.prompt: Write a null hypothesis for an investigation into whether caffeine affects the heart rate of Daphnia. (1)
questions.solution: There is no difference in the heart rate of Daphnia with and without caffeine / caffeine has no effect on heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: State the purpose of a null hypothesis in a statistical test. (1)
questions.solution: It states there is no effect / difference, which the statistical test can accept or reject based on probability [B1]

questions.prompt: Devise a valid investigation using a spirometer to test the hypothesis that people with a larger chest size have a lower breathing rate because their tidal volume is greater. (4)
hints: Measure chest size and spirometer traces.
questions.solution:
Measure chest circumference of each volunteer [B1]
Use spirometer to record tidal volume and breathing rate at rest (soda lime to absorb CO₂, medical-grade oxygen) [B1]
Control age, sex, fitness, smoking, and rest before measuring [B1]
Use a large sample and test for correlation (Spearman's rank) [B1]
Safety: nose clip, sterilised mouthpiece, stop if dizzy [B1]
Any 4 — max 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a spirometer trace can be used to measure the rate of oxygen consumption. (4)
questions.solution:
Soda lime absorbs exhaled CO₂ [B1]
So the volume of gas in the spirometer falls as oxygen is used [B1]
Measure the fall in the trace (troughs or peaks) over a set time [B1]
Rate = volume decrease ÷ time [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use a spirometer to investigate the effect of exercise on breathing rate and tidal volume. (4)
hints: Measure at rest, then after exercise.
questions.solution:
Record trace at rest for a set time [B1]
Subject does a set exercise (e.g. 2 min stepping at a set rate) [B1]
Record trace immediately after; measure tidal volume (peak height) and breathing rate (peaks per minute) [B1]
Repeat with several people / same conditions; safety precautions [B1]

questions.prompt:
A Golgi stack has 6 cisternae, each 15 nm high, with 25 nm gaps between adjacent cisternae.

Calculate the total height of the stack in µm. (2)

A cell membrane is 7 nm thick and a cell is 20 µm in diameter.

How many times greater is the cell diameter than the membrane thickness? (2)
A bacterium has a volume of 1.5 µm³. Express this in mm³ in standard form. (2)

An adult has a mass of 80 kg and contains 1000 g of calcium. 1 % of this calcium is in soft tissue; bone makes up 4 % of body mass.

Calculate the calcium concentration in soft tissue in µg g⁻¹. (3)
hints: Mass of calcium in soft tissue = 1 % of 1000 g.
questions.solution:
Calcium in soft tissue = 10 g = 1.0 × 10⁷ µg [M1]
Soft tissue = 0.96 × 80 000 g = 76 800 g [M1]
1.0 × 10⁷ ÷ 76 800 = 130 µg g⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 250 g sample of leaves contains 42.5 mg of calcium.

Calculate the concentration in µg g⁻¹. (3)
A solution contains 0.5 mol dm⁻³ of a substance. Calculate the volume of this solution and of water needed to make 20 cm³ of a 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solution. (3)
questions.solution:
0.5 × V₁ = 0.1 × 20 [M1]
V₁ = 4 cm³ of stock [A1]
16 cm³ of water [A1]

questions.prompt:
Human soft tissue contains about 130 µg g⁻¹ of calcium, but one plant species contains 170 µg g⁻¹. A student concluded that calcium is more important in plants than in animals.

Evaluate this conclusion. (6)
questions.solution:
Comparison only uses human soft tissue, ignoring 99 % of calcium in bone [B1]
Total calcium per gram of whole body is much higher in humans [B1]
Only one plant species measured, so can't generalise to plants [B1]
Concentration doesn't show importance — calcium has vital roles in both (e.g. muscle contraction, clotting, synapses; plant cell walls / middle lamella) [B1]
No repeats / variation data given [B1]
Conclusion is not valid [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: A small study of 20 people found that those who took a vitamin D supplement for one winter had fewer colds. Evaluate the conclusion that vitamin D prevents colds. (6)
questions.solution:
Small sample size [B1]
No mention of a control / placebo group or blinding [B1]
Other variables not controlled (age, lifestyle, exposure) [B1]
Only one winter; not repeated [B1]
Plausible mechanism — vitamin D supports immune cell function [B1]
Conclusion "prevents" is too strong; need a large randomised controlled trial [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the features of a well-designed double-blind trial of a new drug, and explain why each is important. (6)
questions.solution:
Large sample, so results are representative and anomalies have less effect [B1]
Participants randomly allocated to drug or placebo groups to avoid bias [B1]
Placebo group to control for psychological effects [B1]
Double-blind — neither patients nor doctors know who has the drug, preventing bias [B1]
Groups matched for age, sex, health [B1]
Statistical analysis of results / repeated and peer reviewed [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).
